docs.title: The assistant
docs.description: Operate Flagon by asking. Reads run automatically; changes are proposed for you to confirm.
docs.body:
Flagon is AI-first: anything you can do in the dashboard, you can do by asking
the assistant, and anything the assistant can do, you can also do yourself. It is
built into the platform, not bolted on, so it gains new abilities as the product
grows.

## How it behaves

- **It acts as you.** The assistant runs operations with your identity and your
  organization's scope, so it can never do anything you could not do yourself.
- **Reads run, changes are proposed.** Read-only actions happen immediately.
  Anything that changes data is returned as a proposed action for you to confirm
  first, so you stay in control.
- **It is scoped to Flagon.** The assistant helps you operate Flagon. It is not a
  general chatbot, and it will steer back to what it can actually do.
- **It can read the docs.** Ask it how something works and it searches this
  documentation to answer, rather than guessing.

## Model choice and cost

The model is configuration, not code. Flagon ships with a hosted default and can
point at any OpenAI-compatible endpoint or a self-hosted model, so you can run
your own for a flat cost. Usage is metered per organization so plans can be
enforced.

See [MCP server](/docs/ai/mcp) to give the same abilities to an external agent.

docs.title: MCP server
docs.description: Point an external agent at mcp.flagon.io to operate Flagon and read its documentation.
docs.body:
Flagon exposes a **Model Context Protocol** server at
[mcp.flagon.io](https://mcp.flagon.io), so an external agent (for example, an
assistant in your editor) can work with Flagon directly.

## One registry, three front doors

The MCP server, the in-product [assistant](/docs/ai/assistant), and the HTTP API
all draw from the same set of operations. Add a capability once and it is
available everywhere. Nothing the agent can do reaches around the
permission-checked API.

## What it exposes today

- **Documentation tools.** Any agent can search Flagon's docs and read pages, so
  it can learn how Flagon works before acting. These are read-only and safe to
  use without authentication.
- **Operational tools.** Acting on your organization's data over MCP requires
  authentication, so the agent operates as you, with your scopes.

## Connecting

Point your MCP-capable client at `https://mcp.flagon.io` to get started. With no
credentials, the server exposes only the read-only documentation tools.

To reach the operational tools, present a Flagon access token as a bearer token:

```
Authorization: Bearer flagon_xxx
```

The token acts as you: the server resolves it to your identity and the tools you
can use are exactly the ones your token's scopes allow (a token with no scopes
has full access, still bounded by your role). A tool your token cannot reach is
simply not listed. This is the same permission model as the REST API - the token
is the ceiling, and tenant isolation always applies.

docs.title: Authentication and scopes
docs.description: How Flagon API tokens authenticate and how scopes gate every operation.
docs.body:
Every Flagon API operation is permission-scoped. A token authenticates the
caller and carries a set of **scopes**; an operation runs only if the token's
scopes cover it, and enforcement fails closed.

## Tokens

An access token is minted from the UI or the API and presented as a bearer
token. Tokens act as a user within a single organization: they can never do
anything the issuing user could not do themselves, and row-level security still
applies to every query the token drives.

## Scopes

Scopes are hierarchical: a parent scope implies its children. When you mint a
token you choose its scopes from a grouped checklist, each row labeled with the
raw scope and a one-line description. The vocabulary is shared across the whole
platform, so the same scope means the same thing whether a request comes over
REST, from the in-product agent, or over MCP.

Add a scope when you add an operation. Because scopes are generated from the same
code that generates the OpenAPI spec, this reference stays in lockstep with what
the API actually enforces.

docs.title: Expanding responses
docs.description: Inline related objects in a single request with Stripe-style expand[] parameters.
headings: The project with its organization inlined:
docs.body:
Flagon is a hub for your data, and its objects reference each other - a project
belongs to an organization, an audit event has an actor, and so on. By default a
response returns a **reference** to a related object (an id, like `org_id`), not
the whole thing, so payloads stay small and predictable.

When you need the related object too, ask for it with **`expand[]`** (the same
convention Stripe uses) instead of making a second request.

## How it works

Add one `expand[]` parameter per relation you want inlined. The expanded object
appears alongside the reference it came from.

```sh
# Just the project (org_id only):
GET /orgs/acme/projects/billing-api

# The project with its organization inlined:
GET /orgs/acme/projects/billing-api?expand[]=organization
```

```jsonc
{
  "id": "…",
  "slug": "billing-api",
  "org_id": "org_…",
  // present only because organization was expanded:
  "organization": { "id": "org_…", "name": "Acme", "slug": "acme", "role": "owner" }
}
```

You can expand several relations at once, and the parser is forgiving - repeated
params and comma-separated lists both work:

```
?expand[]=organization&expand[]=created_by
?expand=organization,created_by
```

## Rules

- **Opt-in.** Nothing is expanded unless you ask; the reference id is always
  present whether or not you expand it.
- **Permission-scoped.** An expanded object is only ever returned if your token
  and role could read it on its own - expand never widens access.
- **Unknown expansions are ignored**, so adding an `expand[]` your client
  understands but a given endpoint doesn't is harmless.

Expansion is being rolled out across the API; each operation's OpenAPI entry
lists the relations it supports.

docs.title: Pagination and search
docs.description: How list endpoints page and search - keyset cursors, Link headers, and the HTTP QUERY method.
headings: First page of projects whose name or slug contains "api":
Querying with a request body: the QUERY method
docs.body:
Every list endpoint in Flagon shares one convention: results are **searched on the
server** and returned a page at a time, with the next page reached through a
**cursor**. The rules below are identical for projects, members, teams,
collaborators, owners, invitations, and every other list, so a client that can
page one list can page them all.

## Parameters

A list request takes three optional parameters:

| Param | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `q` | Free-text search. Matched case-insensitively against the human columns of the resource (a project's name and slug, a person's name, email and username, and so on). Omit it for no filter. |
| `limit` | Page size, 1-100. Defaults to 30; values above 100 are clamped. |
| `cursor` | An opaque keyset cursor marking where the previous page ended. Omit it for the first page. |

```sh
# First page of projects whose name or slug contains "api":
GET /orgs/acme/projects?q=api&limit=20
```

## Paging with the Link header

The response carries the rows in its body and, when more results exist, a
[Link header](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8288) pointing at the next page:

```
Link: </orgs/acme/projects?q=api&limit=20&cursor=eyJ2IjoxLCJrIjpbImFwaS1ndyJdfQ>; rel="next"
```

Follow that URL to get the next page; it already carries your `q` and `limit`, so
you only ever hand back the cursor Flagon gave you. When there is no `rel="next"`
link, you have reached the last page.

Pagination is **keyset**, not page-number based: each page resumes exactly after
the last row of the previous one, ordered by a stable key. This stays fast no
matter how deep you page and never skips or repeats a row when the data changes
underneath you. The trade is that there is **no total count or page count** - you
page until there is no next link, rather than jumping to "page 7".

- **The cursor is opaque.** Treat it as a token to echo back, not something to
  parse or build. Its contents can change without notice.
- **A cursor belongs to its query.** Keep `q` (and `limit`) the same as you page;
  changing the search means starting a new sequence from the first page.
- **A malformed or foreign cursor** is rejected with `422`.

## Querying with a request body: the QUERY method

Long searches, or structured filters you would rather not cram into a URL, can be
sent with the **[HTTP QUERY method](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110)**
instead of GET. QUERY is a safe, read-only method that carries its parameters in
the request body. Every list endpoint accepts it at the same path, with the same
three fields in a JSON body:

```sh
QUERY /orgs/acme/projects
Content-Type: application/json

{ "q": "api", "limit": 20, "cursor": "eyJ2IjoxLCJrIjpbImFwaS1ndyJdfQ" }
```

The behavior is identical to the GET form, including the `Link` header on the
response. QUERY is offered for clients that support it; it is not required, and
Flagon's own dashboard uses the GET form. Because QUERY is newer than OpenAPI's
fixed method set, these endpoints are not listed under a `query` verb in the
generated spec, but they are fully supported at runtime.

## Rules

- **Search is always server-side.** There is no "fetch everything and filter"
  path; `q` does the work in the database, so a client never has to hold a whole
  list in memory.
- **Permission-scoped.** Paging and search never widen access: you only ever see
  rows you could already read, and the same token scope that guards the GET form
  guards the QUERY form.

docs.title: Using the API
docs.description: The base URL, how requests authenticate, and the live OpenAPI reference.
headings: The reference is generated from the code
docs.body:
Flagon is API-first: every capability in the product is an HTTP API operation
first, so anything you can do in the dashboard you can do over the API.

## Base URL

All requests go to `https://api.flagon.io`. Most resources are org-scoped, for
example `GET /orgs/<org>/projects`.

## Authentication

Requests authenticate with a bearer token that carries a set of scopes:

```bash
curl https://api.flagon.io/orgs/<org>/projects \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $FLAGON_TOKEN"
```

See [Authentication and scopes](/docs/api/authentication) for how tokens are
minted and how scopes gate each operation.

## The reference is generated from the code

The OpenAPI document is generated from the API's source, never hand-written, so
it always matches what the API actually does. It is served live at
`https://api.flagon.io/openapi.json`, and the interactive reference lives at
[/docs/api](/docs/api).

Because the spec is generated, new endpoints and fields appear in the reference
the moment they ship.

headings: One set of capabilities, three front doors
docs.body:
A quick map of the pieces you will work with. Each has its own page under
[Platform](/docs/platform/projects); this is the overview.

## Organizations

The **organization** is the top-level container. Your projects, members, tokens,
and settings all live inside one, and URLs are org-scoped
(`app.flagon.io/<org>/...`). Your personal account settings at `/settings` are
the one exception.

## Projects

A **project** is a deployable app, the core unit you build on. There is no
separate "app" layer above it. See [Projects](/docs/platform/projects).

## Members and access

People join an organization as **members** with roles, and access is
**permission-scoped** from day one. A token or an agent can only ever do what the
person behind it is allowed to do, and tenant isolation is enforced in the
database, so one organization can never see another's data.

## One set of capabilities, three front doors

The dashboard, the [assistant](/docs/ai/assistant), and the
[API](/docs/api/using-the-api) (and [MCP](/docs/ai/mcp)) all drive the same
permission-checked operations. Whatever you learn one way carries over to the
others.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.description: Flagon is a developer platform for operating your whole system, from the dashboard, the API, or an AI assistant.
docs.body:
Flagon is a **developer platform** for operating your whole system: a single
place to bring your projects and tools together, understand what's happening
across them, and act on it, from the dashboard, the API, or an AI assistant. It's
powerful with AI, and great without it.

Use it hosted at [app.flagon.io](https://app.flagon.io), or run the whole thing
yourself. It is open source and self-hostable end to end.

## The idea

Your work is spread across a dozen tools. Flagon's job is to pull that together
into one system you can operate and reason about, with AI wired through all of it.
The point is not another dashboard to check; it's to ask
_"what changed across everything this week?"_ and get a real answer, grounded in
your actual data.

Everything runs on a few ideas:

- **One place, many surfaces.** Anything you can do in the dashboard you can do by
  asking the [assistant](/docs/ai/assistant), or over the
  [API](/docs/api/using-the-api) and [MCP](/docs/ai/mcp). Same operations, same
  permissions, three front doors.
- **AI over your real data, safely.** The assistant acts as you, with your scopes,
  and changes are proposed for you to confirm. AI is a first-class way to operate
  Flagon, not a bolt-on.
- **Open and yours.** Self-hostable, permission-scoped, and built in the open.

## What you can do today

- Create and manage **organizations** and invite **members** with scoped roles.
- Create **projects** to organize the systems you operate.
- Mint **API tokens** with fine-grained **scopes**, and drive everything
  programmatically or over MCP.
- Ask the **assistant** to do any of the above, and to read these docs, for you.

## Where it's going

Flagon is growing into the hub for your whole engineering system: connected
context across your tools, metrics and insights, agents and orchestration with
humans in the loop, and the governance to run AI safely over real data. Those
areas are marked _Soon_ in the navigation as they land.

## Next steps

- **[Quickstart](/docs/get-started/quickstart)** to get your first project going.
- **[Core concepts](/docs/get-started/core-concepts)** for the model behind it all.
- **[The assistant](/docs/ai/assistant)** to start operating Flagon by asking.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.description: Create your organization and first project, and meet the assistant, in a few minutes.
docs.body:
Get from nothing to a working project in a few minutes. Every step below can be
done in the dashboard, by asking the assistant, or against the API. Pick whichever
fits how you like to work.

## 1. Get an account

Use Flagon hosted at [app.flagon.io](https://app.flagon.io/signup), or run it
yourself. If you would rather self-host, jump to
[Self-hosting Flagon](/docs/self-hosting/overview) and come back here.

## 2. Create an organization

Everything in Flagon lives inside an **organization**: your projects, your
members, and your settings. Create one and you land at `app.flagon.io/<org>`.

## 3. Create your first project

A **project** is a deployable app. Create one from your organization's
dashboard, or just ask the assistant:

> Create a project called `billing-api`.

Read operations run immediately; anything that changes data (like creating a
project) is proposed for you to confirm first, so you stay in control.

## 4. Drive it from the API

Everything you just did is an API operation. Mint a token with the scopes you
need, then call the API:

```bash
curl https://api.flagon.io/orgs/<org>/projects \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $FLAGON_TOKEN"
```

See [Authentication and scopes](/docs/api/authentication) for how tokens and
scopes work, and [Using the API](/docs/api/using-the-api) for the full reference.

## Next steps

- **[Core concepts](/docs/get-started/core-concepts)** for the model behind it all.
- **[Projects](/docs/platform/projects)** for the unit you build on.
- **[The assistant](/docs/ai/assistant)** to do more of this by asking.

docs.title: Adding tools
docs.description: How we decide what software the company runs on: prefer few, boring, and owned over a sprawl of half-used subscriptions.
docs.body:
Every tool a company adopts is a small tax it pays forever: another login, another integration to keep working, another place the truth might live, another bill. A pile of half-used SaaS tools is how a company ends up with its own operations quietly rotting. So we're deliberate about what we add, and the default answer to "should we get a new tool for this?" is "probably not, let's see if what we have already does it."

## What we reach for

- **Fewer tools, used fully,** over many tools, used at ten percent. One thing everyone actually knows beats five nobody has learned.
- **Boring and proven** over new and exciting, the same instinct as [how we build](/handbook/how-we-build). A tool is infrastructure; novelty there is a cost you pay at the worst possible moment.
- **Open source where it's a real option.** We'd rather build on things we can read, fork, and self-host than rent something we can't see inside. It fits how we work, and it's rarely the wrong call.
- **Where the work already lives.** Most of what a company reaches for another tool to do, [GitHub](/handbook/working-in-github) and the handbook already do. Reach there first.

## Before you add one

Adding a tool is a decision the whole company inherits, so make it in the open:

1. **Say what problem it solves,** specifically. "It would be nice" isn't one. A real, recurring pain is.
2. **Check we don't already have it.** We probably pay for something adjacent. Duplicate tools are how one team's data drifts out of sync with another's.
3. **Think about the data.** Where does our information go, who can see it, and can we get it back out? A tool you can't export from is a trap with a monthly fee. Anything touching customer data gets a harder look, see [security](/handbook/security).
4. **Someone owns it.** A tool with no owner becomes a bill nobody remembers and an integration nobody maintains. If you add it, you own it until you hand it off.

<Callout type="note" title="Adding is easy, removing is the hard part">
  It takes a minute to sign up and years to notice nobody uses it. So we treat
  adding a tool as the bigger decision it actually is, and we cull the ones that
  stopped earning their place.
</Callout>

docs.title: Benefits and perks
docs.description: What we offer beyond salary, and the philosophy behind what we do and don't.
headings: The tools to do the job
What we're not going to do
docs.body:
Benefits are where companies love to perform generosity: catered lunches, foosball tables, a wall of logos for perks nobody uses. We're not interested in that. The point of a benefit is to make your life better and get friction out of your way so you can do good work and then go live your life. Everything below is judged against that, not against how it looks on a careers page.

We're small and early, so some of this is intent we're building toward rather than a fully-loaded package today. We'll tell you plainly which is which, because a benefit you can't actually use is just marketing.

## Equity for everyone

If you help build Flagon, you should own a piece of it. Not just the founders, not just the first few, everyone. It's how we [play the long game](/handbook/values) with the people who build the thing.

Everyone gets options on a standard vesting schedule, and we'll be clear about what you're getting and what it could mean, without the hand-waving that usually surrounds equity. The details live alongside the pay framework in [compensation](/handbook/compensation).

## Remote-first, for real

We're [remote-first](/handbook/working-here) by default, not as a reluctant concession. You work from wherever you work best. We optimize for written communication, asynchronous by default, so your calendar isn't hostage to someone else's timezone and you're not punished for logging off to have a life.

## Time off you actually take

The worst version of flexible time off is the one where the policy says "unlimited" and the culture says "don't." We're trying hard to build the opposite: time off that's genuinely encouraged and genuinely taken, with leadership modeling it rather than quietly competing to never unplug. The full thinking, and how we keep it honest, is in [time off](/handbook/time-off).

## The tools to do the job

You can't do good work on a machine that fights you. We set you up with the equipment you need and a real home-office setup, because the cost of good tools is trivial next to the cost of your time and frustration. If something you use every day is slow or broken, replacing it is a good decision, not a favor you have to ask for.

## A budget to get better

We want people who keep sharpening their craft, and that costs money and time. So there's a learning budget for the books, courses, conferences, and tools that make you better at what you do. We'd rather you grow here than stagnate here. The culture around it, spending it without a permission slip and sharing what you learn, is [learning out loud](/handbook/learning-out-loud).

## Health and family

Solid healthcare and real parental leave, because people should be able to take care of their bodies and their families without it becoming a crisis. We'd sooner run lean elsewhere than cut a corner here. We're a young company standing these up properly right now, and each specific goes into the open the moment it's set, which is what the note below is about.

<Callout type="note" title="Where the numbers go">
  The specifics (the learning budget, the equipment allowance, healthcare
  details, leave length) publish right here, each with a real figure, as we set
  them. We'd rather show you the honest state than dress up a number we haven't
  committed to.
</Callout>

## What we're not going to do

We have a bias toward removing friction over adding gimmicks. Given the choice between a perk that photographs well and one that quietly makes your week easier, we'll take the boring, useful one every time.

No ping-pong-table nonsense, no "we're a family" act, no perks designed to keep you at your desk longer. The best benefit we can offer is a job that respects your time, pays you fairly, and gets out of your way. The rest is in service of that. If we ever add a perk that's more about looking good than doing good, that's a bug; the [Discord](https://discord.gg/dtYQs6rPXN) is open.

docs.title: Assets
docs.description: Where the logo lives, the treatments to reach for, and the clear-space and sizing rules for using the mark cleanly anywhere.
docs.body: Everything Flagon makes is in the open, and the brand is no exception. The mark, the palette tokens, and the type choices all live in the source for this site, so the canonical version of the identity is never a stale file in a shared drive: it is whatever is in the repo right now. See [open source](/handbook/open-source) for where that is. ## The mark, canonically The source of truth for the mark is the `FlagonMark` component, which renders crisp at any size and follows the current theme. For anywhere that can't import the component, another app like the product at app.flagon.io, an email, a slide, there are self-contained SVG files hosted at stable URLs. The teal brew is baked in, and the glass outline uses `currentColor` with a light and dark default built in, so they read on any background even when dropped in with a plain `` tag. Do not recreate the mark by hand; use these. - **Static:** [`/brand/flagon-mark.svg`](/brand/flagon-mark.svg) - **Animated** (pours in, then a slow living wave; halts under reduced motion): [`/brand/flagon-mark-animated.svg`](/brand/flagon-mark-animated.svg) - **Mono** (single ink, for tinting to one colour): [`/brand/flagon-mark-mono.svg`](/brand/flagon-mark-mono.svg) Inline the SVG and set a `color` on it to recolour the outline yourself. See the [visual identity](/handbook/brand-visual-identity) page for the treatments side by side. ## Formats - **SVG** is the default for anything digital. It stays sharp and stays small. - **PNG** at 2x or 3x when a raster is unavoidable, on a transparent ground. - **Monochrome SVG** for single-colour contexts, using the mono treatment. If you are producing something physical or high-stakes (an event backdrop, printed swag, a partner placement) and want a second pair of eyes, ask in the Discord before it goes to print. It is cheaper than a reprint. ## Clear space and minimum size - **Clear space:** keep space around the mark equal to at least the height of the lid on every side. Do not crowd it with text or other logos. - **Minimum size:** 16px tall on screen, a little larger in print. Below that the sheen drops away by design and the silhouette still reads. - **Backgrounds:** the mark wants contrast. Put the full or flat treatment on a plain ground; use the mono treatment when the background is busy or a fixed colour. ## Don't The four rules on [visual identity](/handbook/brand-visual-identity#using-the-mark) are the short version. The ones people trip on most: never ship the hollow outline (the brew is the mark), and never stretch, rotate, recolour half of it, or add effects. If you find yourself modifying the vessel, stop and use one of the three treatments instead.

docs.title: Foundations
docs.description: What the brand is built out of: taste over polish, the personality we aim for, and who we are actually talking to.
docs.body:
If [the overview](/handbook/brand-overview) is why brand matters, this is what it is made of. Three things: taste, a personality, and a clear idea of who is on the other end.

## Taste over polish

Polish is surface. Smooth gradients, on-trend layouts, a shadow on everything. It is easy to buy and easy to fake, and skeptical people read it as a tell.

Taste is the thing underneath: a real point of view, and the care to get the small stuff right because it is right, not because anyone asked. The exact wording of an empty state. Whether the spacing is even. What happens when the network drops. Most people will not consciously notice any of it. They feel all of it, and the sum reads as "someone made this on purpose." With generated slop piling up everywhere, that difference is what people are actually responding to.

What taste looks like here:

- **The details are the work, not the polish afterward.** Typography, alignment, the copy on a button, the error nobody plans to hit.
- **Everything on the page earns its place.** If an element has no reason to be there, it goes.
- **We go the extra inch for the person who notices.** More people notice than you would guess.
- **We enjoy it.** When the maker liked making the thing, it shows. When they were phoning it in, that shows too.

## The personality

Flagon should read a certain way, and consistently. A quick calibration:

| We aim for | Not | 
| --- | --- |
| Direct | Fluffy |
| Honest, including about limits | Corporate optimism |
| Plain-spoken | Jargon and fog |
| Dry wit, when it is actually funny | Try-hard jokes |
| Considered | Random |
| Warm | Saccharine |
| Confident | Arrogant |

The failure mode on the left column is trying too hard. The failure mode on the right is saying nothing to avoid being wrong. We would rather have a point and stand behind it.

## Who we are talking to

Mostly builders: engineers and product-minded people who ship things and have been burned by software marketing before. That shapes everything, because these are people who:

- distrust marketing by reflex, and can spot corporate spin in seconds,
- prefer "it does X" to "it empowers you to unlock X,"
- respond well to honesty, including honesty about tradeoffs and what we have not built yet,
- like wit and cannot stand forced humour,
- will read the source, because reading source is fun to them.

The right mental model is not an enterprise buyer or an executive. It is a smart, skeptical friend who builds things. Write to that person. Design for that person. If something would embarrass you in front of them, it is not done.

## Before it ships

Before anything with our name on it ships, run it through one question: **how would this land with a skeptical builder who has seen every trick?** If it would get quietly closed as try-hard or dishonest, change it. If it would earn a nod, ship it. That instinct, applied a thousand small times, is the brand.

docs.title: In practice
docs.description: How the brand shows up on real surfaces: the site, docs, release notes, support, social, and swag. The same instincts, applied everywhere.
docs.body:
The brand is the accumulation of every ordinary interaction, not a page anyone reads before deciding to trust us. It is made or lost in the small, unglamorous surfaces far more than in a hero image. Here is how the same instincts apply where they actually meet people.

## The site

The site is often the first and last impression. Keep it honest and specific. Say what a thing does, in the present tense, without hype adjectives. Lead every page with the real point in the first paragraph. Use the schematic, technical visual system rather than stock photography. If a section exists only to fill space, cut it.

## Docs and release notes

These are read by people mid-problem, so clarity beats personality. Get to the answer fast, show the code, and be exact. A little dry wit is welcome in a release note; none is welcome in a paragraph someone is reading because something broke. Never dress up a limitation as a feature. If something does not work yet the way someone expects, say so and say what to do instead.

## Support

Support reaches someone at the exact moment their trust is up for grabs, which makes it the brand surface that matters most. The rules:

- **Answer like a person who can actually fix it,** because at Flagon the people answering can. No script, no "I'll pass this along" black hole.
- **Be specific, especially with bad news.** Instead of "I'll share your feedback," say why the thing works the way it does and what the person can do next.
- **Fix our own mistakes generously.** If someone gets a surprise bill because our pricing or a default confused them, we make it right. Being right is worth more than the revenue.

## Social and public replies

Every public reply is the brand talking. Be helpful, be human, and do not get defensive when someone is critical, even when they are wrong. If they are being genuinely unreasonable, the move is to be the calmer, bigger party, or to step away. Wit is fine. Punching down, sarcasm at a confused person, and corporate defensiveness are not.

## Swag and physical things

Merch is a thank-you, not an ad. Give it to people who say kind things or show up and help, and make it something they would actually wear or use. A good sticker earns more goodwill than a campaign. A cheap, ugly one costs more than it looks like it should, because it is the brand in someone's hands.

## When something new comes up

New surfaces will keep appearing that none of these pages predicted. The answer is always the same two questions from [the foundations](/handbook/brand-foundations): would this hold up to a skeptical builder looking closely, and would we be happy to be treated this way? If yes to both, ship it. If not, you already know what to change.

docs.title: Overview
docs.description: What brand means at Flagon, why we treat it as a growth engine rather than a coat of paint, and where to find the rest of it.
docs.body:
Brand is not the logo. The logo is a small part of it. Brand is the total of every experience someone has with Flagon: the first paragraph they read on the site, the shape of an error message, how fast we answer a question in the Discord, whether the pricing did what we said it would. Every one of those leaves an impression, and the sum of all of them is the brand. We do not get to decide what it is. We only get to decide what we put in.

We take it seriously for two plain reasons.

**It is how we grow.** We are not going to out-spend anyone on ads, and we do not want to. People recommend Flagon because using it felt honest and the work looked good. A brand people trust is a brand people bring up in a thread without being asked. That is the growth we are building for, and it compounds.

**Trust is slow in and fast out.** It takes a long time to earn someone's belief that we mean what we write, and one lazy headline, one dark pattern, one canned support reply to spend it. So the bar is not "did we ship something." The bar is "would this hold up if a skeptical person looked closely." They will look closely. We want them to.

## The golden rule

Everything in these pages comes back to one idea we use everywhere else too: treat people the way we would want to be treated. If a tactic would give us the ick as a customer, it gives them the ick, so we do not use it, even when it would work. Hold a brand decision up to that and most of them get easy.

## What lives here

This section is the working brand reference for anyone making something with Flagon's name on it, which is everyone.

- [Foundations](/handbook/brand-foundations): what brand is made of here, and the taste behind it.
- [Voice](/handbook/brand-voice): how we sound in writing, with the rules we actually follow.
- [Visual identity](/handbook/brand-visual-identity): the mark, the palette, the type.
- [Assets](/handbook/brand-assets): where to get the logo files and how to use them.
- [In practice](/handbook/brand-in-practice): applying all of it across real surfaces.

If you are deciding something and none of these answer it, the rule above usually does.

docs.title: Visual identity
docs.description: The Flagon mark, the palette, and the type, with the rules for using them. One vessel, one accent, one typeface family.
docs.body:
The visual system is deliberately small: one mark, one accent colour, one type family. Small systems are easier to keep consistent and harder to get wrong, and restraint reads as confidence. It should feel considered, a little technical, and never precious.

## The mark

The mark is a flagon that is actually full. The brew is the mark; the vessel just holds it. It comes in three treatments. Reach for the one that fits the surface, and never redraw the vessel.

<MarkTreatments />

It has to hold from a favicon to a hero. It stays legible down to 16px; below that the sheen falls away gracefully and the silhouette still reads as a full flagon.

<MarkSizes />

The mark isn't only a still image. Pouring is part of it: the brew fills in once, then keeps a slow living wave with a few rising bubbles. Reach for the motion where it earns attention, a hero or a loading state, and the still mark everywhere else. All of it is CSS, and it halts under reduced motion.

<MarkMotion />

## Colour

A single accent, teal, on cool neutrals. The neutrals carry a faint cool bias so they read as chosen rather than default. Dark mode is true black, not a dark grey, so the teal has somewhere to glow. Every value is a design token, so swapping the token re-themes the whole system at once.

<Palette />

The one accessibility rule that bites: the brand teal is only about 3.6:1 on the light background, which fails AA for text. For links and small text on light surfaces, use the deeper `#0f766e`. The bright teal is for marks, fills, and large display only, never body text on white.

## Type

Three roles, kept clean. **Hanken Grotesk** sets headlines: tight tracking, a touch heavier, the display voice. **Geist** carries body and UI, the neutral workhorse. **JetBrains Mono** handles labels, code, and data as its own separate thing. Uppercase captions get wide tracking; headings get tight.

<TypeSpecimen />

## Using the mark

Four rules cover almost everything. When in doubt, give the mark room and keep it full.

<MarkUsage />

For the actual files and formats, see [brand assets](/handbook/brand-assets). For applying all of this to real surfaces, see [brand in practice](/handbook/brand-in-practice).

docs.title: Voice
docs.description: How Flagon sounds in writing: the register we use, the words we avoid, and the rules that keep it consistent across everyone who writes.
docs.body:
Almost all of Flagon reaches people as words: the site, docs, release notes, support replies, the handbook you are reading. Voice carries most of the brand. The chapter on [how we write](/handbook/how-we-write) covers the craft; this is the brand-level register, the sound we are all aiming at so it holds together no matter who typed it.

## The register

Write like a competent person explaining something to a peer they respect. Not a brand. Not a bot. Not a hype man. A person who knows the thing, has nothing to hide, and does not need to oversell.

- **Say the thing.** Lead with what is true and useful. Get to it in the first sentence.
- **Short words, short sentences.** If a plain word will do, use it. Cut the one you would not say out loud.
- **Specific beats grand.** "Answers in a day, usually less" beats "world-class support." Numbers and nouns over adjectives.
- **Admit the edges.** Say what something does not do, or what we have not finished. It reads as trust, not weakness, and it is true.
- **Dry over loud.** Wit lands when it is a little unexpected and genuinely funny. If you are reaching for a joke, drop it.

## Words we do not use

A short banned list keeps the fog out. Avoid:

- **Hype adjectives:** revolutionary, seamless, cutting-edge, world-class, next-generation, game-changing.
- **Filler verbs:** empower, unlock, leverage, supercharge, elevate, delight.
- **Fake urgency:** "act now," "limited time," "don't miss out."
- **Weasel hedges:** "industry-leading," "best-in-class," "trusted by thousands" with nobody named.

None of these carry information. They are the sound of a company talking to itself.

## A few house rules

- **Second person.** Talk to "you," not "users" or "customers," wherever it reads naturally.
- **Contractions are fine.** They are how people talk.
- **No em-dashes or en-dashes in prose.** A comma, colon, or period does the job. This is a house style, and it is deliberate.
- **We are here now.** Write about Flagon in the present, as a company that exists and does what it says. Never "coming soon," "one day," or "when it is real." If something is early, say what is true about it today.
- **Own mistakes plainly.** When we get something wrong, say so in normal words and say what we are doing about it. No corporate non-apology.

## The gut check

Read it back as if a sharp friend sent it to you. Does it sound like a person who knows what they are talking about, or like a company trying to sound like one? If it is the second, rewrite it until it is the first.

docs.title: Bug prioritization
docs.description: How we decide which bugs get fixed when. A simple four-level scheme, honestly applied, so the important things get fixed fast and nothing rots silently in a backlog.
docs.body:
Not every bug is an emergency, and not every bug can wait. The point of having a scheme is so that call gets made deliberately and out loud, instead of by whoever shouts loudest or whatever's freshest in someone's inbox. This is deliberately simple: four levels, a label on the issue, and the honesty to tag things at the level they actually are.

## The four levels

We tag every bug with one of these, as a label on the issue:

| Level | What it means | What we do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **P0** | Critical and breaking: a crash, data loss, something core is down or wrong. | Drop what you're doing. This is the most important thing in the building until it's fixed. |
| **P1** | Urgent but not breaking: it works, badly, or a real workflow is painful. | Fixed soon, ahead of feature work, not left to drift. |
| **P2** | Affects the experience but the thing still functions. | Scheduled into normal work; a real fix, on a real timeline. |
| **P3** | Icebox: minor, cosmetic, or rare. Worth fixing when we're nearby. | Fixed when someone's in the area, or when it climbs the list. |

The levels aren't about how annoyed anyone is. They're about impact on the person using Flagon: how many people, how badly, and whether there's a way around it.

## Tag it honestly

The scheme only works if the labels mean something. The two failure modes are inflating everything to P0 so your thing gets attention, and quietly under-tagging a real problem so it doesn't spoil a roadmap. Both corrode trust in the labels, and once nobody believes the labels, you're back to shouting. Tag it at the level it actually is, and if you think something's mislabeled, say so and change it.

<Callout type="warn" title="A P0 that's live in production is an incident">
  If a P0 is actively hurting users right now, it's not just a high-priority bug, it's an [incident](/handbook/incidents). Treat it as one: stabilize first, fix, then write up what happened. The label and the playbook go together.
</Callout>

## Who decides

Whoever's triaging tags it, and anyone can push back. There's no bug committee. Because you [own what you build](/handbook/feature-ownership), the bugs in your area are yours to weigh, and because we don't build walls between building and support, a lot of these come straight from [support and care](/handbook/support-and-care), where the same question asked three times is one P1 to fix, not three tickets to close.

## Bugs versus features

A backlog of P2s and P3s that never gets touched because features always win is its own kind of bug. We don't let quality rot silently under a pile of new work. The rough rule: P0 and P1 come before feature work, P2s get woven into normal cycles rather than deferred forever, and P3s are the happy tax you pay when you're already editing nearby, which ties back to [fixing the adjacent broken thing](/handbook/feature-ownership). Shipping small and often only stays safe if the small things you shipped actually work.

## Security bugs are different

A security vulnerability is prioritized on its severity like any other bug, but it's handled under a different rule: we don't discuss it in public until a fix is live and reasonably rolled out. The details of how we grade and handle those are in [security and trust](/handbook/security). If you think you've found one, treat it as sensitive from the first moment.

docs.title: Building a team worth being on
docs.description: Why the bar stays high and we hire slowly, and how a great small team beats a big average one.
headings: Keeping the bar high is everyone's job
docs.body:
The biggest lever on whether Flagon is any good is who's on it, not the process or the tooling. A small team of unusually good people who trust each other will out-build a large team of fine ones every time, and it isn't close. So the most important thing we do is keep the bar high and hire slowly, especially when it's tempting not to.

## Talent density over headcount

Every hire either raises the average or lowers it, and on a team this small one wrong hire costs far more than a missing one. We'd rather be short-staffed and stretched than fill a seat with someone who isn't clearly a lift. Growing the team is a decision we make when the work genuinely needs it, not a number we chase to look impressive. See [small by design](/handbook/how-were-structured) for how that shapes the org.

## Craft and character, not pedigree

What we look for barely mentions your résumé. We care whether you can take an ambiguous problem and make something genuinely good out of it, whether you're kind and direct, and whether you'd make the people around you better. Where you went to school and how many years you've clocked tell us almost nothing about that. The full picture is in [how we hire](/handbook/how-we-hire); the point here is that a world-class team gets built one careful, unhurried hire at a time.

## Keeping the bar high is everyone's job

The bar isn't something a hiring manager guards alone. Everyone who interviews owns it, everyone who works alongside a new hire gives honest feedback, and nobody gets waved through because we're busy. It's tempting, when you're underwater, to lower it just this once, and that's exactly when it matters most to hold, because the cost of a wrong hire lands hardest on a small, stretched team. A great place to work is mostly great colleagues; protecting that is protecting the thing itself.

## The deal runs both ways

A team worth being on isn't only a high bar to get in. It's what we owe you once you're here: real ownership, honest pay, room to grow, and colleagues who are actually good. We ask a lot, so we hold up our end. What that looks like day to day is [a world-class place to build](/handbook/engineering-environment) and [growing here](/handbook/growing-here).

docs.title: How we review code
docs.description: Kind and rigorous, fast on small changes, and aimed at the person who reads this code a year from now.
headings: What a good comment looks like
Review for the reader and the long haul
docs.body:
Code review is two people making a change better, not a gate you sweet-talk your way through and not a stage where a senior person performs authority. When it works, the code that lands is better than either person would have written alone, and both of them understand it. This is where a lot of [how we build](/handbook/how-we-build) actually happens, so it's worth being deliberate about. For the step-by-step mechanics, the author's checklist and the reviewer's, see [how we review PRs](/handbook/how-we-review-prs).

## Kind and rigorous, both

These aren't in tension. The kindest thing you can do for a colleague is read their change carefully and tell them the truth about it. Waving through code you didn't understand isn't nice, it's negligent with a smile. Rigor without kindness is just someone showing off; it makes people ship smaller, safer, more timid changes to avoid the ordeal of review, which is the opposite of what you want.

So: high standards, warm delivery. Assume the author is smart and had reasons. Ask before you accuse. The review is about the code, not about them, and your tone should make that obvious.

## Review for real

Read it like you'll maintain it, because you might. That means actually reading it: following the logic, checking the edge the author probably didn't hit, thinking about the call site you can't see in the diff. "LGTM" on 600 lines you skimmed is not a review, it's a signature on a document you didn't read.

If you don't have time to review it properly, say that instead of approving it anyway. A slow review is annoying. A fast approval on code nobody checked is how the 2am page gets written.

## Small PRs get fast reviews

The single biggest thing an author controls is size. A change you can review in ten minutes gets reviewed in ten minutes. A 900-line change sits for two days because nobody has a two-hour block to give it the attention it needs, and when they finally do, they rubber-stamp it out of guilt.

<Callout type="brand">
  Want a fast, thorough review? Send a small change. The two are the same request.
</Callout>

Keep them small, keep them focused, and separate the noisy commits (a rename, a formatting pass) from the real one so the reviewer isn't hunting for signal in a wall of diff.

## What a good comment looks like

A good comment is specific and often a question. It points at a line, names the concern, and where it can, suggests a direction.

```
# useful
This retries forever if the host is down. Cap it, or is there a
reason we want unbounded here?

# less useful
this seems wrong
```

The first invites a conversation and might teach you something (maybe there is a reason). The second is a shrug that makes the author guess what you meant. Say the real thing, say it precisely, and separate "this must change" from "here's a thought" so the author knows what's blocking and what's a preference.

## Review for the reader and the long haul

The person you're really reviewing for isn't the author, it's whoever opens this file in a year with no context and a bug to fix. Optimize for their ability to understand what's here. Naming, a comment that explains the why (not the what), an abstraction that isn't cleverer than the problem: these matter more than local style nits, and they're what review is uniquely good at catching.

## Disagreement, handled well

You will disagree, and that's fine, that's the point. Argue it in the open, on the merits, briefly. Most disagreements dissolve once both people say what they actually mean. When one doesn't, the author usually gets the call on reversible things, since they own what they ship, and you pull in a third person for the genuinely hard, expensive ones. What you don't do is relitigate a settled decision in every future PR, or go quiet and passive-aggressive.

This is [feedback](/handbook/feedback) in one of its highest-leverage forms: frequent, low-stakes, and specific. Treat it that way and it stops being a chore and starts being the best part of the day.

docs.title: How we communicate
docs.description: Async-first, writing over meetings, kind and direct, public by default.
docs.body:
Communication is most of the job. Software is just the residue of a lot of people understanding each other well enough to build the same thing. Here's how we try to do it.

## Async first

We default to async. Not because we dislike each other, but because async is how you get long, uninterrupted stretches to do real work, and how you include people across timezones without making anyone set an alarm.

Async also means most of what we say is written, and writing is a feature. A written message can be read carefully, replied to when someone's actually ready to think, and found again in six months. A meeting evaporates the moment it ends.

## Writing over meetings

When in doubt, write it down. A short doc or a clear message beats a call for almost everything, because it scales to people who weren't in the room and to a version of you that's forgotten the details.

Good writing here is short, specific, and honest about what you're unsure of. You don't need to be a stylist. You need to make the reader's job easy: say the point first, then the reasoning, and don't bury the actual ask three paragraphs down. See [how we work](/handbook/how-we-work) for why we lean on this so hard.

## Public by default

Talk in the open. Public channels beat DMs, comments on the doc beat a private aside, and the [GitHub org](https://github.com/flagon-io) beats a conversation nobody else can see.

The reason is selfish as much as principled: public conversation is searchable, and someone you've never met might have exactly the context you're missing. A DM helps one person once. The same message in the open helps whoever hits the same question next month. Keep private only what's genuinely private: pay, health, performance, and anything about a specific person that isn't theirs to broadcast.

## When to actually talk

Real-time isn't banned. It has a narrow, real use. Reach for a call when:

- A disagreement has gone three rounds in writing and isn't converging.
- Something's on fire and the latency of async is costing you.
- The conversation is emotional, delicate, or just easier said than typed.
- You're new, or working with someone new, and need to build some human rapport.

When you do talk, write down the outcome afterward. The call was for the people in it; the notes are for everyone else. A decision that only the attendees know about isn't really a decision the company made.

## Kind and direct

The tone we're after is kind *and* direct, not one at the expense of the other. Direct without kind is just being a jerk with extra steps. Kind without direct is a slow way of wasting someone's time.

Say the true thing, plainly, and assume the other person can handle it. Skip the compliment sandwich; people can smell the filler, and it makes the real feedback harder to find. How to give it well, and take it well, is its own page: [giving and getting feedback](/handbook/feedback).

## Handling disagreement

Disagreement is a feature. A team that never argues isn't harmonious, it's just not paying attention. We want the argument: early, in the open, about the work.

The rule is that you fight about ideas, not people, and you fight to find the right answer, not to win. Argue your case as hard as you honestly can. Then, when a call gets made, get behind it even if it wasn't yours. That's the disagree-and-commit norm, and it's covered properly in [how decisions get made](/handbook/decisions). Sulking after a decision isn't principled; it's just slow sabotage.

## The community

Discord is where we talk with the people who use and follow the work. It's not a support queue or a marketing channel, but a room where the company happens to be legible.

Talk to the community like you'd talk to a colleague: kind, direct, and honest about what you don't know. If you don't have an answer, say so. If something's a bad idea, say why. People can tell the difference between a company that's listening and one that's performing. Come find us at the [Discord](https://discord.gg/dtYQs6rPXN), or email [hey@flagon.io](mailto:hey@flagon.io) if you'd rather not do it in public.

docs.title: How we pay people
docs.description: The philosophy, the formula, and the levels behind every number we pay.
headings: Fair, transparent, and the same for everyone
Location: market, not cost of living
Equity, reviews, and what comes next
docs.body:
Pay is where a company's values get tested, because it's where the incentives are. Anyone can claim to be fair when nobody's watching the numbers, so we wrote ours down. Here is the whole philosophy and the actual formula behind it, every input visible and none of it going to change.

## Fair, transparent, and the same for everyone

We pay people fairly for the work, and we run the exact same framework for everyone. Your pay is a function of your level and the role, computed the same way it's computed for the person next to you. It is not a function of how hard you pushed in the offer call, whether you happened to hold a competing offer that week, or how comfortable you are talking about money.

Transparency is how we keep ourselves honest. Inside the company, anyone can understand how pay works and roughly where they sit. Secret pay is how quiet unfairness survives: it's a lot harder to underpay someone systematically when the framework is sitting on the table for everyone to check.

## Why we don't negotiate

We make our best offer and we explain how we got there. We don't sandbag the first number so we have room to "come up," and there's no reward for brinkmanship. If you think we've misjudged your level or missed something real about your experience, tell us and we'll fix it. That's a correction, not a negotiation.

This isn't just tidiness. Negotiation looks neutral and isn't. The research is consistent: women and people from underrepresented groups are, on average, less likely to push hard on salary, and more likely to be penalized socially when they do. So a company that pays according to who negotiates hardest is quietly building unfairness straight into its payroll and calling it merit. We'd rather just get the number right the first time, for everyone, than reward the people who happen to be loudest about their own worth.

It cuts both ways. You don't have to be a shark to get paid fairly here, and "another company offered me more" isn't a lever, because we're not pricing against panic. We're pricing against what the role is worth.

## The formula

Every base salary at Flagon comes from the same four ingredients, multiplied together:

**base salary = benchmark x level x step x location factor**

That's it. No secret adjustments, no discretionary fudge factor for people who ask nicely. The **benchmark** is the market anchor for a role. The **level** and **step** place you within that role by scope and by depth. The **location factor** adjusts for the market you work in. Change one input and you can see exactly what changes in the output, which is the point.

## Levels: scope, not status

There are five levels. They describe the scope and impact of the work you're trusted to own, not your title, your tenure, or how senior you sound in a meeting. You level up by doing bigger work, not by waiting your turn.

- **Junior.** You're building your craft. You own well-defined pieces of work and grow fast with support around you.
- **Intermediate.** You own features end to end and need little scaffolding to get from problem to shipped.
- **Senior.** You own ambiguous, important problems and make the people around you better. Senior is the anchor of the whole system, the **1.0** that every other level is expressed relative to.
- **Staff.** Your impact spans beyond your own work: you shape how whole areas get built and set the technical direction others follow.
- **Director.** You own outcomes at the scale of the organization, holding responsibility for how large swaths of Flagon operate and succeed.

Notice these are described by what you're trusted to own, not by status. A Senior who deepens their craft is worth more than a Staff who coasts, and the framework should reflect that. That's what steps are for.

## Steps: depth within a level

Within a level, four steps capture how established you are at that scope. Each step is a band rather than a single point, so your pay lands in a range and can grow without you changing levels at all.

- **Learning.** You're new to this level and still growing into its full scope.
- **Established.** You're solidly operating at this level. This is where you land when you join, by default.
- **Thriving.** You're consistently exceeding what the level asks for.
- **Expert.** You're one of the people others look to at this level, setting the bar for it.

## Location: market, not cost of living

We're [remote-first](/handbook/working-here), and pay does vary by where you are, but not the way most companies do it. We don't dock your pay because your rent is cheap. We follow the local market rate for the work, the way GitLab does it: the location factor reflects what your skills command in your market, not what it costs you to live there.

There's a floor built in, so nobody ends up underpaid for living somewhere the market undervalues. And because it's a published rule applied identically to everyone, it's not a private discount we negotiate person by person, and it's not something anyone can game.

## Try it

Put the four inputs together and you can see a real range. Here's the calculator we use, so you can price out any combination yourself instead of taking our word for it.

<CompCalculator />

<Callout type="note" title="About these numbers">
  These benchmarks are anchored to public market data, so the numbers you see
  are real and honest today, not invented. As we set Flagon's own bands, they'll
  replace these right here, in the open. The formula that turns a benchmark into
  a salary doesn't change.
</Callout>

## Equity, reviews, and what comes next

**Equity for everyone.** Everyone building Flagon gets options on a standard vesting schedule, because the people who make it work should own a piece of what they built. That's part of [playing the long game](/handbook/values) together. The full terms are in [share options](/handbook/share-options), alongside the rest of the package in [benefits](/handbook/benefits).

**Reviews you don't have to ask for.** We revisit pay proactively, a few times a year, so keeping your salary right is our job, not a thing you have to work up the nerve to raise. If the benchmark moves or you've grown into a new level or step, we catch it and adjust. You should never have to schedule an awkward meeting to be paid what the framework already says you're owed.

**Real bands, published.** We hold pay to the same standard as the rest of this handbook: a pay decision that can't survive being written down where the people it affects can read it is probably the wrong decision. That's why the framework is public, and Flagon's own bands land here as we set them. See [how this handbook works](/handbook/how-this-handbook-works).

The direction is fixed and public: fair, legible, and the same for everyone. If you want to argue with the framework, the [Discord](https://discord.gg/dtYQs6rPXN) is open, or email [hey@flagon.io](mailto:hey@flagon.io).

docs.title: Customer comms as an engineer
docs.description: When you ship something that changes what customers experience, they should hear it from us first, clearly, and before it bites them. How to do that well.
headings: When a change needs a heads-up
docs.body:
This is about the messages you send outward, on purpose, when your work changes something a customer relies on. It's the proactive twin of [support and customer care](/handbook/support-and-care), which is about answering when people come to you. A deprecation, a breaking API change, a migration, a pricing or quota change, an incident with lasting effects: in all of these, the worst way for a customer to find out is by hitting it. Telling them first is part of shipping the change, not a nicety that happens later.

## When a change needs a heads-up

Not everything you ship needs an announcement. Most small improvements just land. Reach for proactive comms when a change could surprise someone who's depending on current behavior:

- A breaking change to the public API, the typed client, or the CLI.
- Deprecating or removing something people use.
- A migration that changes data, defaults, or how something works.
- A limit or quota that will start being enforced.
- The lasting aftermath of an [incident](/handbook/incidents), once the fire is out.

If you're unsure whether something clears the bar, it probably does. Erring toward telling people is cheap; a customer blindsided by a change they could have prepared for is expensive.

## Who owns the message

You, the person who made the change, own getting it communicated. That doesn't always mean you personally write the final copy: if someone owns customer comms, loop them in and hand them what they need. But the responsibility for making sure it happens is yours, not something you assume a mailing list will take care of on its own. This is [feature ownership](/handbook/feature-ownership) reaching all the way to the customer.

## What a good notice contains

Whoever writes it, a useful notice is specific and honest, in the [voice we use everywhere](/handbook/brand-voice):

- **What is changing**, concretely, not "improvements to your experience."
- **When**, with a real date, and how much notice they're getting.
- **Why**, briefly, because people extend more patience when the reason is clear.
- **What they need to do**, if anything, with the exact steps or a link to them.

<Callout type="brand">
  Write it for the customer who will be woken up by this change, not for the person who shipped it. If the notice wouldn't have saved you from an unpleasant surprise, it isn't done.
</Callout>

## Aim it precisely

Send it to the people it affects, and ideally only them. Blasting everyone about a change that touches one cohort trains people to ignore you, so that the one message that really matters gets skimmed and deleted. Work out who's actually impacted, the specific accounts or the users of the specific feature, and target that. Precise comms stay trusted; noisy comms get filtered.

## Log it where people look

Beyond the direct message, durable changes belong in the [changelog](/changelog), so there's a public, permanent record someone can find later when they're trying to work out when something changed. Because we [build in the open](/handbook/open-source), a lot of this is visible in the commit history and the roadmap already, but the changelog is where we say it in plain language aimed at the people using the product, rather than the people building it. A good rule: if you sent customers a notice about it, it should be in the changelog too.

docs.title: Deciding what to build
docs.description: How priorities actually get set here: not by a PM ranking a backlog, but by a team that understands its users deciding together, including for products that are already mature.
docs.body:
At a lot of companies, "deciding what to build" is a PM privately ranking a backlog and handing down the top of the list. That's not how it works here, and the difference follows directly from what [product managers](/handbook/product-managers) are for. The decision is the team's, made out of a shared understanding of users and the numbers. The PM's job is to make that understanding rich enough that the decision is close to obvious.

## The inputs, not the authority

Good prioritization comes from holding a few things at once:

- **What users actually need**, from the standing habit of [listening to them](/handbook/listening-to-users).
- **How the product is doing**, from [the metrics](/handbook/product-metrics) and where they're pointing.
- **Where the company is going**, from the [strategy](/handbook/which-products-to-build) and [who we build for](/handbook/who-we-build-for).

A team that genuinely holds those three rarely needs a ranking exercise to know what matters most. When the inputs are clear, the priority usually is too. When the team can't agree, it's almost always because one of the inputs is thin, and the fix is to go get it, not to escalate to whoever has the most authority.

## Validate by building small

We don't try to prove an idea is right before we build it, because [that mostly doesn't work](/handbook/product-engineering). The cheapest way to test most ideas is to ship the smallest real version and watch, which is the whole argument in [ship the smallest useful change](/handbook/iteration). So "deciding what to build" is less about picking the one perfect bet and more about choosing the next small, reversible step that will teach us the most.

<Callout type="brand">
  Prefer the change you can ship this week and learn from over the plan you could defend in a meeting. Real usage beats a convincing argument almost every time.
</Callout>

## Mature products need different questions

A young product is asking "does anyone want this at all." A mature one is asking something else, and the prioritization changes to match. Here the useful questions are about deepening rather than proving: where are users hitting friction, what's quietly holding back retention or expansion, which rough edge would most repay polish, what complexity has accumulated that we could now remove.

Removing things belongs on this list. A feature nobody uses is a cost the whole team keeps paying, so cutting it is real work worth prioritizing, not cleanup you get to someday. The best thing to build is sometimes the thing to delete.

## What we don't do

We don't build for internal alignment over user need: shipping something because it's easier to agree on than the thing that would actually help. We don't spend six months on a big feature before a user can touch any of it. And we don't treat the backlog as a promise. It's a list of maybes, weighed fresh against what we currently understand, not a queue we're obligated to work through in order.

docs.title: How decisions get made
docs.description: Who decides what, disagree and commit, one-way vs two-way doors, and being wrong gracefully.
docs.body:
Most of a company's quality comes down to the quality of its decisions and how cheaply it can undo the bad ones. Here's how we try to make good ones without drowning in process.

## Someone owns it

Every decision has an owner. Not a committee, not a vibe, but a specific person who's accountable for making the call and living with it.

The owner isn't a dictator. Their job is to gather the context, hear the objections, and then *decide*, including deciding against loud opinions when they think those opinions are wrong. A decision that requires everyone to agree isn't a decision, it's a hostage situation. We'd rather one thoughtful person be accountable than have a group diffuse responsibility until nobody is.

Who owns what usually follows who's closest to the work. The person doing the thing generally decides how it gets done. The bigger and more expensive a decision is to reverse, the more it makes sense to pull in the people it affects, and the more the reasoning needs to be written down where anyone can read it.

## Disagree and commit

You're expected to argue. Bring your best objection, as hard as you can make it, before the call gets made. The time to fight a decision is while it's still being decided.

Once it's made, you commit, even if you lost. That's the deal. You don't get to relitigate it in side channels, drag your feet, or say "well, I told you so" when it wobbles. Disagree and commit only works if the commit part is real. It's also what makes the disagree part safe: people argue freely because they know a decision will actually get made and everyone will get behind it.

<Callout type="brand" title="The disagree-and-commit deal">
  Argue like you're right, commit like you were wrong, and write down enough
  that the next person can tell which one you were.
</Callout>

## Write down the why

When a decision matters, we write a short record: what we decided, what we were choosing between, and *why* we went the way we did. Lightweight, a few paragraphs, not a legal brief.

The why is the valuable part. Six months from now, someone will look at the outcome and think "that was obviously wrong." Maybe it was. But without the reasoning, they can't tell whether it was a mistake or a sane call given what we knew then, and they'll waste a week rediscovering a dead end we already walked down. The record is a gift to your future colleagues, one of whom is you.

## One-way and two-way doors

The most useful question we ask about any decision: is this a one-way door or a two-way door?

A **two-way door** is reversible. If it's wrong, you walk back through and try again, cheaply. Most decisions are these, and they should be made *fast*, by the owner, without a big process. Deliberating for a week over something you could undo in an afternoon is its own kind of failure.

A **one-way door** is expensive or impossible to reverse: a public commitment, a data model everything depends on, an architectural bet. These deserve real care: more input, the reasoning written down, a night to sleep on it. The mistake we watch for is treating the two the same. Slow decisions on reversible things, and rushed decisions on irreversible ones, are both how you lose.

## Bringing the community in

We build in the open, so a lot of our thinking happens in front of the [community](https://discord.gg/dtYQs6rPXN). We want that. Public reasoning gets stress-tested by people who don't share our blind spots.

But open isn't the same as decision-by-committee. We'll show the reasoning, ask hard questions, and genuinely change our minds when someone's right. What we won't do is put the direction of the company up for a vote, or pretend the loudest thread is a mandate. Input is a gift. The decision still has an owner, and that owner still has to answer for it.

## When we're wrong

We will be wrong, regularly, in public. That's the cost of deciding fast and shipping real things, and it's a cost we'd rather pay than the alternative: being slow, vague, and wrong anyway with no track record to show for it.

When a call turns out badly, we say so, fix it, and update the record with what we learned. No spin, no quiet edit hoping nobody noticed. A company that can't admit a mistake can't correct one, and correcting them fast is most of what "good judgment" actually is over a long enough run. See [why Flagon exists](/handbook/why-flagon-exists) for why we're playing it that way in the first place.

docs.title: Developing locally
docs.description: Postgres in Docker, then the API and the app however you like: both in containers, or natively so you can keep next dev up while you restart Go. Running in minutes, not days.
headings: api      -> http://localhost:8080   (air live-reloads on Go changes)
The API: defaults point at the compose Postgres, so no env is needed.
It migrates on boot, then serves on :8080.
docs.body:
You should be able to go from a fresh clone to a running Flagon in a few minutes, on your first day, without a wiki-crawl or a colleague on a call talking you through it. Fast, boring local setup is something we protect, because a slow environment is a tax every engineer pays every day. This page is the happy path. If reality doesn't match it, that mismatch is a bug worth fixing, not a rite of passage to endure. The [README](https://github.com/flagon-io/flagon) is the always-current version; this page is the why behind it.

## Before you start

- **Docker**, for Postgres (and optionally the services too)
- **Go** (the version in `api/go.mod`) if you want to run the API natively
- **Node** if you want to run the app natively

That's the whole list. There's no company VPN to join and no private registry to authenticate against. If a setup step ever needs an internal-only credential, we've done something wrong.

## Publish the ports first

The base `compose.yml` binds no host ports on purpose, so it mirrors production and won't collide with a server you're running natively. To do local work, copy the override into place once. It's gitignored, so yours is per-machine:

```bash
cp compose.override.example.yml compose.override.yml
```

`docker compose` picks it up automatically from then on.

## The whole stack in Docker

The simplest way to see everything running:

```bash
docker compose up -d --build
# api      -> http://localhost:8080   (air live-reloads on Go changes)
# app      -> http://localhost:4000   (next dev, live-reloads)
# postgres -> localhost:5432          (databases flagon_api + flagon_app)
```

That's the full system with live reload on both services. The app runs on `4000` here, which conveniently leaves `3000` free for running it natively.

<Callout type="brand">
  One Postgres, two services, live reload. If this doesn't come up clean on a fresh clone, that's the most important bug in the building until it's fixed.
</Callout>

## Or run a service natively

Often you want Postgres and one service in Docker while you iterate on the other by hand, for instance leaving `next dev` up while you restart Go with a plain `go run`. Start just the database, then bring up whichever pieces you're not actively editing:

```bash
docker compose up -d postgres

# The API: defaults point at the compose Postgres, so no env is needed.
# It migrates on boot, then serves on :8080.
cd api && go run ./cmd/flagon serve

# The app: reads app/.env.local automatically.
cd app && npm install && npm run dev   # http://localhost:3000
npm run db:migrate                     # one-time: auth + user_email tables
npm run db:seed                        # a demo user you can log in as
```

## Logging in

`npm run db:seed` (from `app/`) creates a demo account with a static password and a pre-verified email, so you can log in immediately and the tests have stable credentials. It's idempotent, so re-running just resets it. The defaults are `demo@flagon.dev` / `password12345`, overridable with `SEED_*` env vars.

## The flagon CLI

The API binary is the `flagon` CLI. `serve` runs the HTTP API and `migrate` provisions the app role and applies migrations; more commands will follow. Every setting is a flag with an env-var source and a sensible local default, so the common case needs no configuration at all:

```bash
cd api
go run ./cmd/flagon --help          # list commands
go run ./cmd/flagon serve --help    # every flag, env var, and default
```

## Tests

Run the Go tests from `api/`, and lint the app from `app/`:

```bash
cd api && go test ./...
cd app && npm run lint
```

We keep the suite fast on purpose, because a test suite nobody wants to run stops catching regressions, which is the whole argument in [how we test](/handbook/testing). If the tests are slow enough that you're tempted to skip them, that's a real problem worth raising, not a personal failing.

## When setup fights back

If you hit a wall, the fix is almost never to suffer through it quietly. Ask in the engineering channel, and once you're unstuck, improve the thing that tripped you: a clearer error, a missing check, a line in the README or this page. The best possible outcome of a rough first setup is a pull request that makes the next person's setup smooth. We [own what we build](/handbook/feature-ownership), and the developer experience is part of what we build.

Next, get your bearings with [project structure](/handbook/project-structure).

docs.title: Diversity and belonging
docs.description: Why a mix of people makes the work better, and the daily habits that make a small company somewhere you actually want to be.
headings: A mix of people makes the work better
Hire to widen the door, not tick a box
Belonging is a thing you build daily
Paying fairly is part of this
docs.body:
We're small. Small enough that we can't hide behind a diversity report or an affinity-group org chart, and we wouldn't want to. What we can do is say clearly what we believe and hold ourselves to it while the crew is still small enough that every hire moves the whole average. This page is that commitment, written down early so we can be caught not living up to it later.

## A mix of people makes the work better

This isn't charity and it isn't a quota. A room where everyone has the same background, the same schools, the same defaults, is a room with the same blind spots repeated in every chair. You ship the bug none of you could see because none of you have ever hit it. You write the empty state that makes perfect sense to people exactly like you and reads as hostile to everyone else.

Different lives produce different questions. Someone who has been the person a product wasn't built for asks better questions about who yours leaves out. That is not a soft benefit. It shows up in the code, the copy, the support queue, and the decisions we don't regret in three years. It's our [long-term thinking](/handbook/values) applied to who's in the room.

## Hire to widen the door, not tick a box

When we [hire](/handbook/how-we-hire), the goal is to widen the set of people who could plausibly get the job, not to backfill a demographic line. That means writing job posts that describe the work honestly instead of a wish list that only one narrow career path could satisfy. It means not requiring a pedigree as a proxy for skill. It means looking in more than one place, because the same three networks return the same three kinds of people.

Then we judge everyone by the same bar. Widening the door and lowering the bar are different things, and we do exactly one of them. A fair process that more people can enter beats a "diverse" hire made to feel good about a number, which is condescending to the person hired and useless to the work.

<Callout type="note" title="Why we don't wave numbers around">
  At our size, one hire swings every percentage wildly, so we don't wave numbers around as proof of anything. We'd rather point at the process and let you check whether it's fair.
</Callout>

## Belonging is a thing you build daily

Diversity is who's in the room. Belonging is whether they can do their best work once they're in it, and it isn't a poster or a Slack emoji.
