It's built or eroded in small moments: whose ideas get built on and whose get talked over, who gets the benefit of the doubt in a code review, who ends up doing the invisible glue work that never shows up in a promotion case.

So we pay attention to the small stuff. We give [feedback](/handbook/feedback) to everyone, because withholding the hard, useful note from someone is its own quiet exclusion. We write things down and default to public so that being in the right DM at the right time isn't the price of being included. We assume good faith and we say the real thing kindly.

## Paying fairly is part of this

You can't claim to value people and underpay the ones with the least leverage to argue. We tie belonging to money on purpose: our [compensation](/handbook/compensation) approach is meant to be legible and consistent, so pay tracks the work rather than who negotiated hardest or who a manager happened to like. Fair, boring, defensible pay is one of the least glamorous and most real diversity commitments a company can make.

We're at the start of this, not the end. As we grow, the test is whether these hold when they cost something. If you catch us falling short, that's a bug. Say so, in the [Discord](https://discord.gg/dtYQs6rPXN), on [GitHub](https://github.com/flagon-io), or at [hey@flagon.io](mailto:hey@flagon.io).

docs.title: Writing docs as an engineer
docs.description: Docs are part of the product, not a chore that comes after it. Stripe is our north star.
headings: Docs are part of the product
Write for someone trying to get something done
Keep docs close to the code so they stay true
Great docs are a real advantage
docs.body:
Good documentation is a feature, and we treat it like one. The docs are where a lot of people meet what we make: they arrive stuck on something specific, and the docs either get them unstuck or send them somewhere else. Stripe is our north star here, not because their prose is fancy but because their docs respect the reader's time and clearly took real work. That's the bar.

## Docs are part of the product

The docs are not the thing you write once the "real" work is done. They're part of the real work. A feature that nobody can figure out how to use isn't finished, no matter how clean the code is. So we plan for the docs alongside the thing they describe, and we don't call something shipped until a person could actually pick it up from the page.

That framing changes how it feels to write them. Docs aren't a tax on building; they're the last mile of building. The person who couldn't have shipped without understanding the thing is exactly the person who can explain it.

## Write for someone trying to get something done

Nobody reads docs for fun. They're in the middle of a task, slightly annoyed, and they want the answer. So we write for that person: what are you trying to do, here's the shortest honest path to doing it, here's the thing that'll trip you up. We lead with the task, not with a tour of every option nobody asked about yet.

Show, don't tell. A working example a person can copy, run, and adapt beats three paragraphs describing it. Real code, real values, the actual shape of the thing. Explanation is for the parts an example can't carry on its own.

<Callout type="note" title="Write for the stuck reader">
  Picture someone with your docs open in one tab and a half-built thing in the
  other, close to giving up. Write for them. Everything else is decoration.
</Callout>

## Keep docs close to the code so they stay true

The fastest way to lose trust is a doc that's confidently wrong. Docs drift from reality the moment the code moves and the page doesn't, and stale docs are worse than none: they cost someone an afternoon before they realize the page is lying. So we keep docs close to the code they describe, treat them as part of the same change, and update the page in the same breath as the behavior.

When a doc lives next to what it documents, keeping it true is part of shipping instead of a separate cleanup nobody signs up for. This is one more reason we build [in the open](/handbook/open-source): docs in the open are docs people will notice when they go wrong, and that pressure keeps them honest.

## Great docs are a real advantage

Docs are one of the few places where doing the boring work well is genuinely rare, which makes it worth doing. When your docs are clear, people get further on their own, trust what they read, and remember that you didn't waste their afternoon. That compounds. It's cheaper than any amount of marketing and it's hard to fake, because you can feel the difference between docs someone cared about and docs someone resented.

So we hold docs to the same standard as everything else we make: plain, specific, opinionated, and finished. Writing them is [how we build](/handbook/how-we-build), not a chore that happens after. When the docs are worth reading, so is the thing they describe.

docs.title: A world-class place to build
docs.description: What makes Flagon a genuinely great place to be an engineer: autonomy, real ownership, and time to do it right.
headings: Good tools and a fast local setup
Own what you build, end to end
docs.body:
Engineers can work anywhere, so the question we take seriously is why a good one would choose to build here. The answer can't be a foosball table or a mission statement. It has to be the actual daily experience of the work: what you get to do, how much of it is real building versus overhead, and whether the place lets you do the best work of your career. Here's what we've built for that, and what we protect.

## Autonomy that's real

You own decisions, not just tasks. We tell you the problem and the constraints, and then we get out of the way. Nobody here is going to sit over your shoulder specifying which function to write. If you need to be micromanaged you'll be miserable, and if you don't, you'll get to actually think. That trust is the default from day one, not something you earn by surviving a probation ritual.

## Ship to production fast

The distance between an idea and it being live for users is short here, and we work hard to keep it short. You can have code in production on your first day. That's a deliberate consequence of how we build, described in [how we build](/handbook/how-we-build): small changes, a trunk that stays releasable, and boring, reliable deploys. Fast shipping isn't recklessness. It's what you get when the path to production is clean enough that releasing feels routine.

## Minimal red tape

We keep process to the smallest amount that actually helps. There's no committee to petition before you can try something, no six approvals to change a config, no ticket about the ticket. The goal is that on any given day, the overwhelming majority of your time goes into the work itself.

## Good tools and a fast local setup

You should be able to clone the repo and be [running locally](/handbook/developing-locally) in minutes, not fight the environment for two days before you write a line. We invest in that: fast setup, fast tests, fast feedback loops. Slow tooling is a tax paid by every engineer every day, so we treat a sluggish build or a flaky local environment as a real bug worth fixing, not a fact of life to endure.

## Own what you build, end to end

You build it, you own it, from the first commit through it running in production. That means you get the whole arc: the design, the implementation, the deploy, and the satisfaction of watching real people use the thing you made. Ownership isn't a burden we hand off to someone else once the fun part is done. It's the point. The person who built it understands it best, and that understanding matters most exactly when it counts.

## Room for craft and taste

We care how the work is made, not just that it ships. There's room here to name a thing well, to delete the awkward abstraction, to make the code a pleasure for the next person to read. Taste is welcome. We don't mistake motion for progress, and we don't punish the extra thought that separates something that merely works from something that's genuinely good.

## Humane on-call, no hero culture

<Callout type="warn" title="We don't reward heroics">
  A 2am save after a preventable outage is not a highlight, it's a signal that something upstream failed. We fix the system, not lionize the firefighter.
</Callout>

On-call is real but it's humane. The load is shared, the pager is reasonable, and nobody is expected to be permanently reachable or to run on adrenaline. When something breaks, we handle it honestly and calmly: figure out what happened, fix it, and write down what we learned so it doesn't happen twice. Incidents are about the system that let it happen, not about finding someone to blame. Blameless is the only version that actually makes the software more reliable, because people tell the truth when they're not bracing for punishment.

## Time to do it right

Everything above depends on one thing: we don't run people at a permanent sprint. Sustainable pace isn't a perk, it's how you get good software over a long stretch instead of fast software followed by burnout and turnover. We'd rather ship a little less this week and still have a sharp, rested team next year. Doing it right takes time, and we give it.

docs.title: Feature ownership
docs.description: You build it, you own it, from the first commit through it running in production. What that means, and what it doesn't.
docs.body:
Ownership here is simple to state and does a lot of work: the person who builds something keeps an eye on it. We don't write code and throw it over a wall to a separate team that catches the pager when it breaks. The one who wrote the thing understands it best, and that understanding is worth the most exactly when something is on fire.

## What owning it means

- **You see it through to production.** Ownership doesn't end at merge. It ends when the thing is live and working for real users, and honestly it doesn't fully end even then.
- **You watch it.** You know whether the thing you shipped is actually being used, and you notice when it starts misbehaving before a user has to tell you.
- **You improve it.** The first version is rarely the last. Following up to make it better is part of the job, not a nice-to-have you get to if there's time.
- **You keep it honest.** If it changes the API, the typed client and the spec move with it. If it has docs, the docs are true. If it has a page in this handbook, that page still matches reality.

This is the same idea as [product engineering](/handbook/product-engineering): you own an outcome, not a ticket.

## What it does not mean

Owning something is not suffering alone with it. Ask for help early and often; that's a sign of judgment, not weakness. Ownership means the buck stops somewhere real instead of dissolving into "the process," but the work itself is still a team sport.

<Callout type="warn" title="Ownership is not territory">
  Owning a piece of the product doesn't make it yours to guard. Anyone can fix a typo, send a patch, or ask hard questions about your code. If you find yourself defending a boundary instead of a decision, something has gone wrong.
</Callout>

## Fix the adjacent broken thing

A subtle but important part of ownership: when you're in an area and you spot something broken next to your work, you don't step around it and file a ticket for later. You fix it, or at least you make it visible and make sure someone will. Waiting for someone else to fix an adjacent problem is exactly the habit we're trying not to have, described in [how to do product as an engineer](/handbook/product-engineering).

## When ownership needs to move

People change teams, and things change hands. When that happens, ownership transfers deliberately, not by quietly going stale: the new owner actually understands what they're taking on, and the old owner is around long enough to answer the questions that only surface once you're holding it. An owned thing with no real owner is one of the more dangerous states a system can be in, precisely because everyone assumes someone else has it.

docs.title: Giving and getting feedback
docs.description: How we give feedback that helps, how we take it well, and why it's part of working in the open.
headings: Kind and direct, at the same time
Praise in public, criticize in private
Feedback is part of working in the open
docs.body:
Feedback is how a small company stays sharp. When there are only a handful of you, there's no layer of management to catch problems or polish rough edges, so the quality of the work depends on people telling each other the truth, kindly and often. Most teams say they want honest feedback and then flinch every time they get it. We'd rather build the habit for real. This page is how.

## Kind and direct, at the same time

The trap most people fall into is thinking kind and direct are opposites, so they pick one. Pick kind and you get vague reassurance that helps nobody. Pick direct and you get someone who's technically right and exhausting to work with. The skill is holding both: care about the person enough to tell them the actual thing.

Kind and direct means you say the real problem plainly, and you say it because you want the work and the person to be better, not because you enjoy being right. The tone is warm, the content is honest, and you don't dilute the content to protect the tone.

## Timely, specific, about the work

Feedback has a shelf life. The best time to say something is close to when it happened, while the details are fresh and the person can still do something with it. Feedback saved up for weeks and delivered in a batch lands like an ambush, and half of it is stale anyway.

Be specific. "This section is confusing" is more useful than "great job," and "this section is confusing because it introduces the API before explaining what it's for" is more useful than both. Keep it about the work, not the person. There's a real difference between "this function is hard to follow" and "you write confusing code." One is a fixable observation about a thing on the screen. The other is a verdict about a human being, and it makes people defensive instead of better.

<Callout type="brand" title="Good vs bad, concretely">
  Bad: "Honestly this whole approach is kind of a mess." Good: "I got lost around the third step. Could we split the validation out so the happy path reads top to bottom?" Both are critical. Only one tells the person what to do next.
</Callout>

## How we receive it

Getting feedback well is a skill too, and it's the one that makes the whole thing sustainable. If people get punished for speaking up, even with a sigh or a defensive rebuttal, they stop, and then you're flying blind.

When you're on the receiving end, assume good intent. The person took a risk and spent effort to help you, so start from the belief that they're trying to make the work better, because they almost always are. Ask questions if it's unclear. You don't have to act on every piece of feedback, but you do have to actually hear it. Thank people for it, sincerely. "Thanks, that's a good catch" costs you nothing and keeps the door open for the next person.

## Praise in public, criticize in private

Praise is better with an audience. When someone does good work, say so where others can see it, in the channel, in the review, in the notes. It's genuine, it's contagious, and it tells everyone what good looks like here.

Criticism is the reverse. The correction itself lands better one to one, without a crowd, where the person can absorb it without also managing how they look in front of everyone. The exception is technical critique of shared work, a design or a pull request, which lives in the open by nature. Even there the rule holds: the comment is about the design, not the designer.

## Feedback is part of working in the open

We build in the open, which means our disagreements and our course corrections are visible too, in review threads and issue discussions and the [communication](/handbook/communication) we keep public. That's not a bug. Watching people give and take honest feedback in public, and stay collegial doing it, is one of the more useful things an outsider can learn about how we work. It only works if the feedback is real. A handbook full of nice words about candor, contradicted by comment threads full of "LGTM," would fool no one. We do the actual thing, in [how we work](/handbook/how-we-work) and everywhere else.

docs.title: Getting together
docs.description: Remote-first means being in one room is deliberate, not default: what we get together for, and what we don't.
headings: Why bother being in a room
docs.body:
We're remote-first, and we mean it: the company is built to run without anyone being in the same place. That's a feature, not a compromise. But remote-first isn't remote-only, and the fact that we work apart most of the time is exactly what makes the occasional in-person time worth doing well. When being in one room is rare, you have to be deliberate about what it's for.

## Why bother being in a room

If we can do the work async, and we can, then the reason to fly people to one place isn't the work. It's the things that are quietly harder over a screen: reading a room, trusting someone you've only met in pull request comments, having the conversation everyone's been politely avoiding.

You can be perfectly effective with a colleague for a year and still not really know them. That gap is small until the day something's tense, and then it's the whole game. A little face-to-face buys a reservoir of goodwill you spend later, on the hard days, without noticing. That's what we're actually there for.

## What these gatherings are for

Our version of an offsite is small, because we're small. Think a few days, the whole crew, somewhere without a status meeting in sight. The point is connection and the conversations that are hard to have well in text:

- **The tension nobody's raised.** The disagreement that's too nuanced for a thread, easier to work through when you can see each other's faces.
- **The big, fuzzy questions.** Where we're headed, what we're not doing, the stuff that benefits from a whiteboard and a long walk more than a document.
- **Just knowing each other.** Meals, terrible jokes, the unstructured hours where trust actually gets built. This is not filler around the "real" agenda. It is the agenda.

<Callout type="warn" title="Not a status meeting with better catering">
  If a session could have been a doc, it should have been. We don't spend rare,
  expensive in-person time reading updates at each other. Save the room for what
  only the room can do.
</Callout>

## What they're not for

The failure mode of getting together is recreating the office: packing the days with presentations, demos, and roadmap readouts that would have been better as writing. That wastes the one thing an offsite has that a normal week doesn't.

We keep the structured part light and protect the unstructured part fiercely. No one should leave feeling like they attended a conference. The measure of a good gathering isn't how much we covered; it's whether people came back knowing each other better and pulling in the same direction.

## How this fits the everyday

Getting together isn't a substitute for [staying human](/handbook/staying-human) day to day; it's the punctuation on it. The habits that keep us connected between trips, treating people like adults with lives, leaving room for the non-work parts of being coworkers, matter far more in total, simply because there's far more of them.

Think of it as two halves of the same thing. The daily habits keep the relationships warm across distance and time zones. The occasional room resets them deeper than a screen can reach, and then we go home and the daily habits carry it forward. Neither works alone. One without the other is either all warmth and no depth, or a nice week that fades by the following month.

We won't do this often, and that's the point. Rare and deliberate beats frequent and hollow. When we do get together, it's because there's something worth being in a room for, and we treat the time like it cost something, because it did.

docs.title: How we set goals
docs.description: A few real goals over a long list: outcomes over output, revisited often, kept lightweight on purpose.
headings: A few goals, not a list
Why we keep it this light
docs.body:
Most goal-setting is ritual for its own sake: quarterly ceremonies, cascading spreadsheets, a scoring meeting that produces more anxiety than direction. We don't do that. We're small, and small teams have an advantage here that bigger ones would kill for: everyone can hold the whole picture in their head. Our job isn't to build machinery that keeps a hundred people pointed the same way. It's to pick a few things that matter and stay honest about whether they're working.

## A few goals, not a list

We'd rather have three goals we actually mean than fifteen we recite. A long list isn't ambition, it's avoidance: it lets everything feel important so nothing has to be chosen. Choosing is the point.

At any given time we're carrying a handful of real goals, the kind you could say out loud in one breath. If we can't name them without reading off a document, we have too many. When something new looks urgent enough to add, the question is what it replaces, not where it fits.

## Outcomes, not output

A goal is something that changes in the world, not a pile of work we did. "Ship five features" is output. "A new user can get to their first real result without asking us for help" is an outcome, and it's a much better goal, because you can hit the first one and still have built the wrong thing.

Output is easy to measure and easy to fake. Outcomes are harder to pin down and worth the trouble anyway. We tie goals to what a user can now do, what got faster, what stopped breaking. The work is how we get there, not the thing we're grading.

<Callout type="note" title="A goal you can't tell you missed isn't a goal">
  If there's no honest way to know whether we hit it, it's a wish. Write goals so
  that in a few months you could say plainly: yes, no, or here's what we learned
  instead.
</Callout>

## We revisit, we don't ceremonialize

Goals meet reality and reality usually wins. A goal that made sense in the spring can be quietly irrelevant by summer, and pretending otherwise just to protect the plan is how teams march confidently in the wrong direction.

We revisit goals often and lightly. Not a heavyweight quarterly review with scores and a slide deck, just a regular, honest look: is this still the thing? Is it moving? If a goal is dead, we say so and drop it without ceremony. Changing your mind in public when the facts change is a strength, and it connects straight to how [decisions](/handbook/decisions) get made and unmade here.

Dropping a goal isn't failure. Failure is dragging a dead goal through three more months to avoid saying it's dead.

## Goals connect to the direction

None of this floats free. Our goals are the near-term expression of [where we're going](/handbook/where-were-going): the long arc broken into pieces small enough to actually pursue this month. If a goal doesn't ladder up to that direction, it's either a distraction or a sign the direction needs updating. Both are worth catching early.

That link runs both ways. The direction tells us which goals are worth setting; the goals, hit or missed, tell us whether the direction still holds. When enough goals point somewhere the stated direction doesn't, we change the direction, not the reality.

## Why we keep it this light

We keep goal-setting deliberately lightweight, and that's a choice, not a gap we'll fill once we're "mature." Heavy process here would buy us coordination we don't need at this size and cost us the thing we most rely on: the ability to change course fast when we learn something. Small batches and short cycles run through [how we work](/handbook/how-we-work) for the same reason.

When we grow to the point where a few shared goals in everyone's head stops being enough, we'll add exactly as much structure as the problem earns, and not a page more. Until then, a few real goals, honestly revisited, is the whole system.

docs.title: Growing here
docs.description: How you develop and progress at Flagon: by scope, not tenure, and without being forced into management.
headings: Management is a role, not a rung
docs.body:
Growing here means taking on bigger, harder, more ambiguous work over time, and getting better at it. That's the whole model. We don't have a promotion committee, a points system, or a calendar that decides when you're allowed to level up. You grow by doing more, and the framework catches up to you.

## Progression is scope, not tenure

Your [level](/handbook/compensation) describes the scope and impact of the work you're trusted to own, not how long you've been here or how senior you sound in a meeting. So progression is simple to describe and hard to fake: you start owning bigger, fuzzier problems and making the people around you better, and at some point everyone can see you're operating a level up. Then we adjust your level and your pay to match, proactively, without you having to build a case for it.

That cuts both ways. Time served earns nothing on its own, and a title isn't a trophy you're owed for sticking around. What moves you is the work getting bigger. It also means there's no ceiling waiting for a headcount slot to open: if the scope is there, the level follows.

## Management is a role, not a rung

The usual career ladder forces good builders into management to keep climbing, losing a great engineer to gain a mediocre manager. We don't. Management here is a different kind of work someone takes on because the team needs it, not a prize for being good at building. You can grow all the way up by getting deeper and broader at the craft and never manage a soul. See [how we manage](/handbook/how-we-manage) for what that role actually is.

## How the growth actually happens

Nobody grows from a performance-review form. It happens in the work, so we try to make the work the teacher.

- **Real ownership, early.** The fastest way to grow is to own something that matters and be trusted to figure it out. We hand out problems, not tickets, on purpose.
- **Straight feedback, continuously.** You'll hear where you stand from the people you work with and in your [one-on-ones](/handbook/one-on-ones), not once a year in a formal review. See [giving and getting feedback](/handbook/feedback).
- **Room to learn on the clock.** Learning the thing the work needs is part of the work, not something you're expected to do only on your own time. Reach for the book, the course, the conference, the afternoon spent understanding a system properly.
- **Support to stretch.** When you take on something over your head, that's the point, and you'll have people around you to lean on. [Staying human at a distance](/handbook/staying-human) is part of how we make sure stretching doesn't tip into drowning.

<Callout type="brand" title="If you're not growing, that's a problem to raise">
  You should be getting better at something here. If you feel stuck, flat, or
  bored, that's worth saying out loud in a one-on-one. Sometimes it means new
  work, sometimes a new focus. Either way it's a real conversation, not a thing
  to quietly resent until you leave.
</Callout>

docs.title: Have a point of view
docs.description: Generic is the real risk. We would rather make deliberate, opinionated choices than blend in safely.
headings: Sameness is the risk you don't notice
Taste is part of the job
docs.body:
Generic is the real risk, and it's the one that never trips an alarm. Nobody complains about beige. Nobody remembers it either. Most companies drift toward the average because the average is defensible, then wonder why nothing they make lands. We would rather be distinctly ourselves and occasionally wrong than inoffensive and invisible.

## Sameness is the risk you don't notice

Blending in feels safe because no single choice looks reckless. You pick the same stack, the same layout, the same rounded-corner tone as everyone else, and each decision is individually reasonable. Added up, they make something nobody has a reason to care about. The slow slide into generic is how most products die, quietly, of no cause anyone can point to.

So we treat sameness as a cost, not a default. When a choice is up for grabs, "what does everyone else do" is a data point, not the answer.

## Conviction over consensus

Have opinions and be willing to be disliked for them. A product that a smaller group loves beats one that a larger group finds fine, because fine doesn't get talked about, defended, or missed when it's gone. We'd rather make a call, say why, and own it than sand every edge off until there's nothing left to disagree with.

This is not an excuse to be contrarian for sport. The goal isn't to argue; it's to actually decide something, in a direction, with a reason. See [operating principles](/handbook/operating-principles) and [how decisions get made](/handbook/decisions) for how we hold that line without turning every choice into a debate.

## Taste is part of the job

Character isn't a coat of paint you add at the end. It comes from caring about the parts most people skip: the empty state, the error message, the wording of a button, the weight of a line. Taste is just a lot of small decisions made by someone who cared, and it's one of the few things that's genuinely hard to copy. We hire for it, we protect it, and we give people the room to apply it. Craft is how personality earns its place, rather than being announced.

<Callout type="brand" title="Put a competitor's logo on it">
  If a competitor could put their logo on the thing we just made and nobody
  would notice, we haven't finished. Make it unmistakably ours.
</Callout>

## Distinct, not a costume

There's a difference between a point of view and a gimmick. Quirk for the sake of attention wears off fast and usually covers for a lack of substance. We're not interested in being weird to seem interesting; we're interested in being clear about what we believe and letting that show. The mark of it isn't a wacky office or a mascot. It's that our choices are legibly ours, made on purpose, and they hold up when you ask why.

Distinctiveness that comes from conviction lasts. Distinctiveness that comes from wanting to be noticed does not.

## Where this shows up

In the product, in the writing, in this handbook, in the [brand](/brand). Anywhere we're tempted to reach for the default, that's the moment to ask whether the default is actually right or just easy. Usually it's worth the extra thought to make something that could only have come from us. It's part of why we build [in the open](/handbook/values): if the work is going to be visible, it may as well be worth looking at.

docs.title: How our teams work
docs.description: The company Flagon is built to be, told through the teams that run it.
headings: Every team is a little startup
One person or ten, the page stays true
How a team gets its mandate
docs.body:
This is the company Flagon is built to be, described through the teams that run it: what a team owns, how it spends its days, and how the whole thing stays coherent without much process. [Small by design](/handbook/how-were-structured) explains why we stay small; this goes a level deeper, into how a team actually works. For the current shape of the company, see the [teams page](/teams).

## Every team is a little startup

The unit here is a small team that owns something whole, and each one runs like its own little startup inside the company. It has a mission, a lot of rope, and the freedom to figure out how to do the work. It isn't handed a backlog and told to burn it down. It's handed a problem worth solving and trusted to solve it.

That framing does real work. A startup owns its outcome, not just its output: it talks to the people it serves, decides what matters and what to ignore, and moves without asking permission for every step. We want each team to feel that way, because that's when people do their best work and care about the result like it's theirs, which it is.

## One person or ten, the page stays true

A team here might be a few people, or one person wearing the hat for now, or a group that's still filling out. We're not apologizing for that. It's the plan: we grow into this shape on purpose, adding people to a team when the work clearly needs them and not before.

We describe a team by what it owns and how it works, not by how many sit on it. Engineering ships in the open whether that's one person or a dozen. Design holds the taste bar whether or not the title is on anyone's door yet. Read each page as the design, true whether the team is one person today or ten later.

## How a team gets its mandate

A team's mandate is a problem to own, not a list of tickets. Someone can say, in a sentence, what this team is for and how we'll know it's working. That clarity does the work: when a team knows what it owns, it can make its own calls about how to get there, and tell the difference between the work that matters and the work that just looks busy.

Mandates come from the work and the people closest to it, not from a plan handed down and defended. When a team's shape stops matching the problem, we change the shape. See [how decisions get made](/handbook/decisions) for who makes which call.

## Autonomy without drifting apart

Small autonomous teams could easily drift into a dozen companies that happen to share a logo. We keep that from happening without heavy management, mostly by being loud in public. Work happens where people can see it: in [GitHub](https://github.com/flagon-io), in [Discord](https://discord.gg/dtYQs6rPXN), in this handbook. When the reasoning is out in the open, teams stay aligned by reading each other instead of by sitting in a meeting about alignment.

The glue is shared, too. Everyone works from the same [values](/handbook/values) and [operating principles](/handbook/operating-principles), builds on the same product, and holds the same bar for quality. That shared floor is what lets us hand a team the rope and trust it not to wander off. Autonomy isn't isolation; it's freedom inside a set of things we all agree on.

If a team ever feels boxed in, or so loose it's lost the thread, that's a bug. Say so, on [GitHub](https://github.com/flagon-io) or at [hey@flagon.io](mailto:hey@flagon.io). The team model is something we keep tuning, not a thing we set once and walk away from.

docs.title: How this handbook works
docs.description: The handbook is the company: it lives in git, anyone can change it with a pull request, and every page is a draft.
headings: It's the source of truth, not a summary
docs.body:
The handbook is the company. If a process isn't written here, it isn't really how we work yet, no matter how many times someone said it out loud. This page is the mechanics: where it lives, who can change it, and what to do when a page is wrong.

## It's the source of truth, not a summary

There is no shadow version of Flagon that these pages approximate. How we work, how we decide, how we pay people: it is here, or it isn't real. A process that lives only in someone's head, or a chat thread, or "how it's always been done" is a bug we haven't fixed yet. The fix is to write it down, so the next person doesn't have to reconstruct it by asking around.

<Callout type="brand" title="Would you write it down with your name on it?">
  Before something becomes "how we do things," we ask exactly that. If not, we
  don't do it. It's the same filter we apply to pay, to the roadmap, to
  everything.
</Callout>

## Anyone can change it

The handbook lives in [git](https://github.com/flagon-io). Changing how Flagon operates isn't a matter of catching the founder in a good mood; it's a matter of opening a pull request. You edit the page, say why in the description, and it gets reviewed and discussed like any code change. The same process that keeps bad code out keeps bad policy out, and it lets a good idea from anyone become the actual rule without a meeting. A handbook you can only read is a poster; one you can send a pull request to is how a small crew keeps improving the company in public.

## Every page is a draft

This handbook is perpetually unfinished, on purpose. Some pages are thorough, some are a heading and two sentences, and a few are probably wrong right now. A rough page that exists beats a perfect one somebody is still privately drafting and never ships. Found something wrong or missing? Open a pull request against the page. Not ready to write it yourself? Open an issue on [GitHub](https://github.com/flagon-io) or say hi in [Discord](https://discord.gg/dtYQs6rPXN), and someone will pick it up.

docs.title: How to be useful here
docs.description: A short mutual contract on how we show up for each other and get things done.
headings: If it's broken and you can fix it, fix it
Being wrong out loud beats being silent
Leave it better than you found it
docs.body:
Whether you're on the team or you found us through the [code](https://github.com/flagon-io), being useful here looks roughly the same. This is less a to-do list and more a contract in both directions: here's how we expect people to show up, and how you can expect us to show up back. It's warm, and it has teeth.

## Try to help yourself first

When you hit a wall, take an honest swing at it before you ask. Read the [handbook](/handbook/how-we-work), search the code, check the issues. Timebox it, though. Fifteen minutes stuck is learning; two hours stuck is just stubbornness with extra steps. When the timer's up, ask.

Ask in the open. Drop it in the [Discord](https://discord.gg/dtYQs6rPXN) or the issue, not a DM. A question answered in public helps the next person who gets stuck on the same thing, and there's always a next person.

<Callout type="note" title="The timebox is a real number">
  Pick one before you start, five minutes or an hour depending on the size of
  the thing, and honor it. It stops you from either interrupting too soon or
  suffering in silence too long.
</Callout>

## If it's broken and you can fix it, fix it

You don't need permission to make something better. If you spot a typo, a broken link, a confusing paragraph, a bug with an obvious fix, fix it and open the change. The person who noticed the problem is usually the best-placed person to solve it, and "someone should really deal with that" is how nothing gets dealt with.

This goes double for the handbook itself. If a page is wrong, the page is the bug. Edit it. You will not get in trouble for improving something.

For anything bigger than a paper cut, still just start. Open a draft, sketch the fix, show your work. It's far easier for people to react to something real than to a hypothetical.

## Default to public

Work where people can see it. Open the pull request early, think out loud in the issue, write the thing down where others can find it. Private progress feels safer and helps no one. See [how we work](/handbook/how-we-work) for the mechanics of this.

Being public means being visibly unfinished sometimes, and that's fine. A rough draft in the open beats a polished one nobody knows exists.

## Being wrong out loud beats being silent

If you have a hunch, say it. If you think a decision is off, say that too, in the [right place](/handbook/decisions) and with your reasons. We would much rather you be wrong in public and get corrected than sit on a good instinct because you weren't sure.

Silence isn't caution, it's just information we don't have. The cost of a wrong idea said plainly is a two-minute correction. The cost of a right idea never said can be a lot more.

## Ship over asking permission

Bias toward action. If you're reasonably sure and the change is reversible, do it and tell people, rather than asking first and waiting. Most of what we do is reversible, and the ones that aren't are usually obvious. When in doubt, read [how we decide](/handbook/decisions) for where the line sits.

Asking permission feels responsible. Often it's just moving the risk onto someone else's plate. Own the call.

## Leave it better than you found it

The small stuff compounds. Tidy the thing next to the thing you came to fix. Rename the confusing variable, add the missing sentence, delete the dead code. Nobody's assigning this, which is exactly why it matters.

If any of this sounds like your kind of place, come say hi at [hey@flagon.io](mailto:hey@flagon.io) or in the [Discord](https://discord.gg/dtYQs6rPXN). Read [working here](/handbook/working-here) for the fuller picture.

docs.title: How we build
docs.description: The engineering habits we actually keep: ship small, stay releasable, and prefer boring tech that works.
headings: Tests where they earn their keep
docs.body:
This is how we write and ship software. None of it is clever. Most of it is the stuff everyone agrees with in the abstract and then quietly abandons the first time a deadline gets close. We try not to abandon it. These are habits, not rules, and the point of writing them down is so we notice when we're drifting.

## Ship small and often

Big changes are where bugs hide and momentum dies, so we keep them small. A change that takes a day to review is a change nobody reviews well.

Small also means shippable. We'd rather merge a rough first version that does one thing and improve it in the open than sit on a perfect branch for three weeks. The feedback you get from something real beats the feedback you imagine from something planned.

## Main stays releasable

`main` should be deployable at any moment. Not "after we fix that one thing," but now. If it's not, that's the most important problem in the building until it is.

This is what makes shipping small actually work. When the trunk is always green, releasing is uneventful, which is exactly what a release should be. If you're about to merge something you wouldn't want deployed by accident, it's not ready.

## Review for real

Code review is two people making a change better. Read it like you'll have to maintain it, because you might.

Say the real thing. "This is confusing" is a useful review comment. "LGTM" on 600 lines you didn't read is not. When you're the one being reviewed, remember the review is about the code, not about you. There's more on this in [how we review code](/handbook/code-review).

## Tests where they earn their keep

We test the things that would hurt if they broke: the logic that's easy to get subtly wrong, the paths money and data flow through, the bugs we've already been bitten by once. We don't chase a coverage number for its own sake.

A test that never fails is telling you nothing. A test suite so slow nobody runs it might as well not exist. Write the tests that catch real regressions and delete the ones that just make the suite heavier.

## Boring tech, on purpose

Prefer the proven thing. The database everyone understands, the framework with ten years of answered questions behind it, the pattern that's dull because it works. You get a small number of interesting-technology bets in a company, and you should spend them where they actually matter, not on the plumbing.

<Callout type="note" title="Before you adopt something new">
  Ask what it buys you that the boring option wouldn't, and who's on call at 2am when it breaks in a way nobody has seen before.
</Callout>

## Delete code happily

The best pull request is often the one that removes more than it adds. Dead code still gets read, maintained, and worked around by every person who comes after you. If a feature is gone, delete the code. If a branch is never taken, delete it. Git remembers so you don't have to.

Less code means less surface area for bugs and less to load into your head before you can change anything. Treat deletion as progress, because it is.

## Own what you ship

You build it, you keep an eye on it. We don't throw work over a wall to some other team who catches the pager when it breaks. The person who wrote the thing is the person who understands it, and that understanding is worth the most exactly when something's on fire.

Owning it doesn't mean suffering alone. Ask for help early and often. It means the buck stops somewhere real instead of dissolving into "the process."

## Simplicity is a feature

Every layer, option, and abstraction is a tax someone pays later, usually you, six months from now, having forgotten why it's there. Reach for the simplest thing that could work, and add complexity only when reality forces your hand, not because you're anticipating a future that may never arrive.

If you can't explain how it works in a couple of plain sentences, that's a signal. Simple isn't the easy version. It's the version you had to think harder to get to.

This all connects to [how we work](/handbook/how-we-work) and our [values](/handbook/values). Because we're [building in the open](/handbook/open-source), you can watch us succeed and fail at every one of these in the commit log.

docs.title: How we design
docs.description: Design is the whole shape of the thing, not a coat of paint at the end. This is how we think about craft.
headings: Design is the shape, not the skin
Sweat the parts most people skip
Taste is a discipline, not a mood
Design and engineering are one conversation
docs.body:
Design at Flagon isn't the part where someone makes it pretty before launch. It's the shape of the thing itself: what it does, how it behaves when you're confused, what it asks of you and what it does on your behalf. By the time you're picking colors, most of the real design decisions are already made or already blown. We treat design as a way of thinking about the whole product, and we hold it to the same standard as the code underneath it.

## Design is the shape, not the skin

You can put a beautiful surface on a confused idea and it's still a confused idea. Layout, flow, the words on the buttons, what happens when nothing has happened yet: those are design, and they're decided long before anything gets styled. So we start with the shape. What is this for, who's in the middle of doing something when they reach it, and what's the shortest honest path through it?

If the underlying model is wrong, no amount of polish saves it. If the model is right, a plain version of it already works. Get the bones right first.

## Sweat the parts most people skip

The character of a product lives in the moments nobody demos. The empty state before you've done anything. The error copy when something breaks. The first five minutes, when a person is deciding whether this thing respects their time. Most teams leave those to last, or to nobody. We treat them as the work.

An empty state is a chance to teach instead of a blank shrug. An error message is a chance to tell the truth instead of hiding behind "something went wrong." Spend real attention there, because that's where taste actually shows up. This is the same idea as [have a point of view](/handbook/have-a-point-of-view): character comes from caring about the parts most people skip.

<Callout type="brand" title="Not done until it's unmistakably ours">
  If a competitor could ship the same screen and nobody would blink, it isn't
  done yet. The details are where it becomes ours.
</Callout>

## Taste is a discipline, not a mood

Taste sounds like something you either have or you don't, but in practice it's a habit: a lot of small decisions made by someone who cared, and who kept asking "is this actually good, or just done?" We treat it as a discipline you practice, not a vibe you're born with. That means looking at the thing with fresh eyes, cutting the option that's there out of habit, and being willing to redo the part that technically works but feels wrong.

It also means having an opinion and being able to say why. "It feels off" is a start; the job is to find what's off and fix it. Taste that can't explain itself is just preference, and preference doesn't hold up under a "why."

## Design and engineering are one conversation

We don't hand a finished mockup over a wall and wait for it to come back built. Design and engineering are the same conversation, running from the first sketch to the last edge case. The person building it will find the constraint the mockup ignored; the person designing it will catch the interaction the code got lazy about. Both of those are the work getting better, not someone stepping on toes.

Small changes are how this stays honest. A shape you can see running tells you more than a shape you argued about in the abstract, which is exactly why we [ship the smallest useful change](/handbook/iteration) and adjust from something real. Design isn't a phase that ends. It's how we build, and it connects straight to [how we build](/handbook/how-we-build): boring where boring wins, opinionated where it counts, and always closer to something you can actually hold.

docs.title: How we get users
docs.description: Distribution by being genuinely useful and building in the open, not by buying attention or gating the door.
docs.body:
We'd rather earn attention than rent it. That shapes almost every choice about how people find Flagon and decide to trust it.

## The culture is the marketing

Building in public, the open source, this handbook, the honest writing: that is the distribution strategy. People who have never used Flagon can already read exactly how the company runs and how we think, and that earns more trust than any campaign we could buy. See [open source and building in public](/handbook/open-source) for why it's the whole plan.

## Bottom-up and developer-led

The person who feels the problem finds Flagon, tries the free tier for real, and brings it into their org because it made their week better. No demo wall in front of the product, no sales call to get started, no gate between a curious person and the thing working. Adoption starts with one person solving one real problem, and grows from there.

## We earn word of mouth

The best distribution we have is someone telling a colleague "this actually fixed the thing." You only get that by being genuinely useful and honest, over and over, including when it's inconvenient. We optimize for the person in front of us being glad they used it, and trust that a lot of small, real recommendations beat one loud, bought one. Why that recommendation is the whole growth strategy, and not just one channel among many, is [its own chapter](/handbook/making-users-happy).

## What we won't do

No dark patterns, no manufactured urgency, no growth tricks that only work because someone wasn't paying attention. If a tactic would give us the ick as a user, it's out, no matter what it would do to the numbers this quarter.

docs.title: How we got here
docs.description: Flagon's scrappy origins, and the companies we openly learned from.
docs.body:
Chase Pierce started Flagon after enough years inside software companies to know how they usually go: a good idea gets sanded down by process, honest work gets wrapped in language nobody believes, and the gap between what a company says and what it does widens every quarter until the two are barely on speaking terms. Most of that is habit, copied from the company before. Flagon is the attempt to build the other thing, in daylight.

The handbook came before there was much to put in it, and that was deliberate. Writing down how we wanted to work, in public, forced the thinking to be real and gave anyone, inside or out, a way to hold us to it. The company has grown into the document rather than the other way around.

## What shaped us

We didn't invent any of this. A handful of companies figured out how to do it well before we existed, and we studied them closely. The trick is to take a thread from each, not a blueprint from any one of them, because copying a single company page for page just gets you a worse copy of it. Here's open credit for what we borrowed.

**GitLab** treats its handbook as a product: thousands of pages, versioned in git, editable by anyone, with a compensation model you can read instead of negotiate in the dark. We took the handbook-as-product, and pay you can reason about.

**Basecamp / 37signals** made the case for the calm company, small on purpose and unbothered by the hype cycle. Their Shape Up method taught us to fix an appetite and shape the work rather than groom an endless backlog; its fingerprints are all over [how we plan](/handbook/how-we-plan).

**PostHog** proved a handbook can have a pulse: public, opinionated, funny in places, and honest about money down to a public pay calculator. We took the nerve to publish before everything is perfect.

**Stripe** made craft something you could feel in the product, and set the documentation bar the whole industry now measures against. We took craft as a real value and docs as part of the product.

**Linear** showed that taste scales, with opinionated defaults and polish in every corner. We took taste as something you build in from the start, not a coat of paint at the end.

**Valve** showed that capable people, given room, find the important work without a manager assigning it. We took the flat structure and the trust it runs on, which shapes [how we're organized](/handbook/how-were-structured).

<Callout type="note" title="Credit where it's due">
  None of these companies asked to be on this page. Hiding your influences is
  just insecurity with a press release; we would rather point at the people who
  proved this was possible.
</Callout>

Where all of it lands is in [our values](/handbook/values) and [how we work](/handbook/how-we-work). If you want to talk, we are on [GitHub](https://github.com/flagon-io), in [Discord](https://discord.gg/dtYQs6rPXN), and at [hey@flagon.io](mailto:hey@flagon.io).

docs.title: How we hire
docs.description: What we look for, how the process runs, and how offers and rejections work.
docs.body:
Hiring is the highest-leverage thing a small company does. A great hire makes everyone around them better; a bad one costs far more than the salary. We take it seriously, and we try to make the process feel like the company: plain, honest, no games. Here's how it actually works, so there are no surprises.

## What we look for

We're small, so everyone we bring on has to be able to run without a lot of scaffolding. That means a few things matter more here than they might elsewhere.

- **Self-directed.** You can take an ambiguous problem, figure out what "done" looks like, and get there without someone standing over you. We don't hand out tickets and check your homework.
- **Craft.** You care about the work being genuinely good, not just closed. You sweat the parts users never see, because that's where good and fine part ways.
- **Kind and direct.** You can tell someone their idea has a hole in it without making them feel small, and you can hear the same about yours. Direct isn't a license to be a jerk, and kind isn't a reason to stay quiet.
- **Allergic to busywork.** You'd rather ship something real than perform being busy. Status meetings, vanity metrics, and polish-for-show make you itch.

None of this is about pedigree. We don't care where you went to school or how many years you've clocked. We care whether you can do the work and whether we'd want to do it with you.

## The process

We keep it short and we keep it legible. You'll always know what stage you're in and what comes next. The [full sequence, stage by stage, is here](/handbook/the-hiring-process); the shape of it is:

- **A real conversation.** Not a trivia quiz. We talk about what you've built, how you think, and what you're looking for. You should be interviewing us just as hard.
- **A paid work-sample.** Instead of whiteboard puzzles you'll never use again, we pay you to do a small, realistic slice of the actual work. You keep the money regardless of the outcome. It's the fairest signal we know of, for both sides: you see what the work is really like, and we see how you think when it's real.
- **Time with the team.** A couple of focused conversations with the people you'd actually work alongside, so the fit gets checked from more than one angle, in both directions.
- **A decision, quickly.** We don't leave people hanging. When we've made up our minds, you'll hear from us, one way or the other.

We don't play the games. No take-it-or-leave-it exploding offers, no "we have other candidates" pressure, no artificial urgency designed to rush you into a yes. If a company has to trick you into joining, that tells you something, and we'd rather you notice.

<Callout type="note" title="Work-sample, not free work">
  The trial is a scoped, paid exercise built to be a fair test, not a way to get
  a real feature shipped on the cheap. If it ever starts to look like the latter,
  that's a bug in our process. Call it out.
</Callout>

## How offers work

When we make an offer, the number isn't a mystery and it isn't a negotiation. Pay at Flagon comes out of a published formula that's the same for everyone, so the offer is simply what the [compensation](/handbook/compensation) framework says the role is worth at your level. We'll show you the math.

That means no reward for brinkmanship and no penalty for being bad at self-promotion. If we've misjudged your level or missed something about your experience, tell us and we'll correct it. That's a fix, not a haggle. A competing offer isn't a lever here, because we price against what the role is worth, not against panic.

If you want the fuller picture of what you'd be signing up for day to day, [working here](/handbook/working-here) lays it out.

## How we say no

Most of the people we talk to, we won't hire. That's just the math, and it's not a judgment on you as a person. When the answer is no, we try to make it a clean no: a real reason, delivered with respect, and soon enough that you can get on with your life.

We won't ghost you, and we won't hide behind "we've decided to move forward with other candidates" when we can tell you something useful instead. Getting a no from us should still leave you thinking well of us. If it doesn't, we did it wrong.

docs.title: How we interview
docs.description: For anyone running an interview here: how to get a real signal, stay fair, and treat the candidate the way we'd want to be treated.
docs.body:
Interviewing well is a real skill, not something you wing. This page is for whoever is on the other side of the table. The job is to get the strongest honest signal about whether this is a good fit, in both directions, without wasting the candidate's time or tripping over your own biases.

## Get signal, not performance

The point of an interview is to understand how someone actually thinks and works, not to watch them perform under artificial pressure.

- **Go deep, not wide.** A long checklist of questions asked rapid-fire gets you shallow answers to all of them. Pick a few themes that matter for the role and dig into each until you actually understand how the person reasons. One real problem explored properly beats ten skimmed.
- **Use real work.** Talk about things they've actually built, and lean on the [paid work sample](/handbook/the-hiring-process) rather than trivia. How someone approaches a realistic slice of the job tells you far more than whether they can invert a binary tree on a whiteboard.
- **No gotchas.** Trick questions, riddles, and puzzle-box interviews mostly measure who has seen the puzzle before. They make us look clever and tell us nothing. Drop them.
- **Let silence sit.** Give people room to think. The first answer is rarely the most interesting one, and rushing to fill the pause cuts off the good stuff.

## Keep it fair

An interview that isn't consistent isn't a measurement, it's a vibe, and vibes are where bias walks in.

- **Same themes for every candidate** for a given role, so you're comparing like with like instead of comparing your mood on Tuesday to your mood on Thursday.
- **Write down what you saw**, with specifics, right after, before the halo of a good first impression rewrites your memory. Evidence, not adjectives.
- **Watch your defaults.** We're trying to find people who can do the work and who we'd want to do it with, full stop. Pedigree, accent, whether they remind you of yourself: none of that is the job. If you can't tie a reservation to the actual work, it isn't a reason.
- **Decide as a group, on the evidence.** No single person's gut is the verdict. We compare notes and reason it out together, so one loud opinion doesn't carry a hire or a no.

## Respect the person

However it goes, the candidate should come away thinking well of us. They're trusting us with their time and, often, real hope.

- **Sell honestly.** Tell them the good and the annoying. Overselling to close someone just moves the disappointment to month two.
- **Leave time for their questions**, and answer them straight. An interview they can't interrogate back is a bad interview.
- **Give a real answer, quickly.** When it's a no, make it a clean no with a reason. See [how we hire](/handbook/how-we-hire) for how we handle that.

<Callout type="brand" title="If you'd hate it as a candidate, don't do it">
  Every tactic here comes back to one question: would it make you feel small,
  tricked, or jerked around if you were the one being interviewed? If so, leave
  it out.
</Callout>

docs.title: How we make money
docs.description: The actual business model: a genuinely free, self-hostable core, and paid plans for the people who'd rather we run it for them.
headings: Revenue from people glad to pay
docs.body:
A company that can't explain how it makes money is usually hiding something, so here it is plainly. Flagon is open source and self-hostable, and it always will be. We make money from the people who'd rather not run it themselves, and from teams big enough to need the things that only matter at scale. That's the whole model. The pricing philosophy, why it's cheap and stays cheap, gets its own page in [priced below cost, on purpose](/handbook/priced-below-cost); this one is about where the revenue actually comes from.

## Open core, honestly drawn

The product is open source and you can run it yourself for free, forever. We charge for the hosted version, where we operate it for you, and for the capabilities a larger organization needs: scale, controls, the operational load you'd rather hand off.

The line between free and paid is the whole game, and we draw it honestly. The free thing has to be genuinely useful on its own, not a crippled demo engineered to push you into paying. If self-hosting Flagon solves your problem completely and you never pay us a cent, that's a success, not a loophole. We're betting that enough people, given a free option that actually works, will still choose to pay us to take the hosting off their hands.

## Usage-based, and self-serve

You pay for what you use, and you can start, grow, and leave without talking to a salesperson. No annual contract you have to sign before you can try the thing, no "contact us for pricing," no quote that depends on how much they think you can afford. The price is public and the meter is honest.

## Revenue from people glad to pay

The healthy kind of revenue comes from people who'd be a little sad if we vanished: they use the thing, get real value, and think the price is obviously fair. That's who the business is built around. It means we never have to trap anyone, because the people paying us are doing it on purpose and would do it again.

<Callout type="brand">
  We'd rather make less per customer and keep far more of them, glad, than squeeze the ones we have until they resent it. A business that only holds customers because leaving hurts has already lost the argument on the merits.
</Callout>

## Sustainable on purpose

This model only works if it keeps the lights on, and we take that seriously; the discipline behind it is in [staying alive](/handbook/staying-alive). But the point of being sustainable isn't to maximize what we extract. It's to never be so desperate that we're tempted to. A company that isn't worried about next month doesn't need to reach for the dark patterns, and that freedom is worth more to us than the margin we'd gain by using them. How that conviction turns into actual prices is the subject of [priced below cost, on purpose](/handbook/priced-below-cost).

docs.title: How we manage (and don't)
docs.description: What the management job is here, what it isn't, and why it's not a promotion.
docs.body:
Management at Flagon is a job, not a rank. It's a small, mostly-context-providing role that some people do because they're good at it and the team needs it, not a trophy you win for sticking around. This page is about that role itself. For how the teams are shaped, see [how we're structured](/handbook/how-were-structured).

## Management is not a promotion

In a lot of companies, the only way up is to stop doing the thing you're good at and start managing people who do it. We think that's a waste, and it quietly punishes great builders by turning them into mediocre managers.

So here, becoming a manager is a sideways move into a different kind of work, not a step up a ladder. It comes with more context and more responsibility for other people, not more status. Nobody outranks anybody. A manager is a teammate with a particular job, same as the person who owns the database or the docs.

<Callout type="brand" title="No empire building">
  Headcount under you is not a scoreboard. We're not impressed by a big team,
  and growing one for its own sake is a good way to make yourself less useful,
  not more.
</Callout>

## What a manager actually does

Mostly three things: unblock, give context, and grow people.

**Unblock.** When someone's stuck on something they can't move alone, a decision that needs making, a door that needs opening, a fire that needs a grown-up, the manager clears it. The measure of the job is how rarely people are stuck waiting.

**Give context.** A small company moves on shared understanding, not instructions. A manager's real product is context: why this matters, what we're actually trying to do, what changed. People who have the context make good calls on their own. People who don't need to be told what to do, and that doesn't scale and isn't fun for anyone.

**Grow people.** Notice what someone's good at and point them at more of it. Give the feedback nobody else will. Help them get better at the craft and get paid more for it. See [feedback](/handbook/feedback) for how we do the honest part of that.

Notice what's not on the list: assigning tasks. We hand people problems and room, not a queue. If you find yourself doling out tickets, something's gone wrong, either the person doesn't have enough context or you're managing too tightly.

## You can grow without managing

This is the important one. You do not have to manage anyone to grow in impact, seniority, or pay. The most senior person on a team might manage nobody at all. Depth of craft, the size of the problems you can own, the trust you've earned: those move your career and your compensation, with or without direct reports.

If you want to manage because you genuinely like growing people and holding context, good, we need you. If you're eyeing it only because it looks like the next rung, don't. The rung doesn't exist. Go be great at the thing instead.

## Managers are accountable too

A small management job is still a real one. Managers get feedback like everyone else, and pointed feedback at that, because a manager having a bad month affects more people than a builder having one. If your manager isn't giving you context or isn't unblocking you, that's a bug worth [raising](/handbook/feedback), and raising it is not a career risk here. Doing this in the open means the role can be questioned like anything else.

If you're weighing whether this kind of work fits you, [working here](/handbook/working-here) and our [values](/handbook/values) are the honest backdrop.

docs.title: How we part ways
docs.description: How we handle people leaving, by choice or not, with honesty and respect.
headings: What we owe you on the way out
How we try to do it
Leaving well means you're still part of the story
docs.body:
Everyone leaves eventually. People move on, priorities change, sometimes a fit that was right stops being right. How a company handles the door on the way out tells you more about it than how it handles the welcome. Here's how we try to do it, whether you're leaving by choice or we're the ones ending it.

## It shouldn't be a surprise

If we're the ones deciding to let someone go, the reasons should already be familiar. We believe in the ongoing kind of [feedback](/handbook/feedback) that means nobody gets blindsided by their own exit. If something isn't working, you'll hear it early and clearly, with a real chance to change it, long before it becomes a conversation about leaving.

A firing that arrives out of nowhere is usually a failure of the months before it, not a decision made on the day. We'd rather have the uncomfortable conversation early than the devastating one late.

Sometimes it still doesn't work out. That's allowed. Not every good person and every small company are a fit forever, and saying so kindly is better than pretending otherwise.

## What we owe you on the way out

Clarity and dignity, at a minimum. If we're ending it, you get a straight answer about why, said to your face, not buried in process or dressed up as a "reorganization." If you're leaving by choice, you get our genuine thanks and help landing well.

Either way, we handle the practical things without drama: your final pay, whatever's yours to keep, a clean handoff of the work, and references we actually mean. Nobody gets marched out or made to feel like a security threat for having quit.

<Callout type="warn" title="How severance works">
  When we end someone's time here for reasons short of serious misconduct, you
  get real severance: enough to give you room to breathe and find the next
  thing, not a token. We're putting the exact terms in writing on this page, in
  the open like everything else, and the commitment behind them is firm.
</Callout>

## How we try to do it

Clear and kind at the same time. Those aren't opposites. The kindest version of hard news is the honest one, delivered like you're talking to an adult you respect, because you are.

That means real reasons, not corporate fog. A conversation, not an ambush. Enough notice and support that you can land on your feet. No walking-you-out spectacle, no pretending it's mutual when it isn't. If we made the call, we'll own it out loud. That's [how we work](/handbook/how-we-work), applied to the hardest moment.

We'll also be honest about what we got wrong. Often an exit has fault on both sides, or is nobody's fault at all. Saying so is part of the respect.

## Leaving well means you're still part of the story

People who leave Flagon well don't stop being part of it. We build in the [open](https://github.com/flagon-io), so much of what you touched keeps your fingerprints on it whether you're here or not, and we'd rather stay proud of having worked together than pretend it didn't happen.

The industry is small and memory is long. Someone who left years ago might be the person who sends us our next great teammate, or becomes one again themselves. We'd like every exit to be one where that stays possible.

If you're leaving, thank you, honestly. Stay in touch: [hey@flagon.io](mailto:hey@flagon.io) and the [Discord](https://discord.gg/dtYQs6rPXN) doors stay open. And if you're reading this while deciding whether to join, [working here](/handbook/working-here) is the fuller picture of the whole arc.

docs.title: How we plan
docs.description: Small batches, short cycles, and plans that survive contact with reality: cadence without ceremony.
headings: Plans that survive contact with reality
docs.body:
Planning has a bad reputation, and mostly it's earned. Too many teams confuse planning with prediction: an elaborate up-front document that's obsolete the moment real work touches it, defended long past the point of usefulness because someone spent a week on it. We plan differently, and lightly, for the same reason we do most things here: the goal is to keep moving in the right direction, not to produce an artifact that looks like control.

## Short cycles, small batches

We plan in short cycles, on the order of a couple of weeks, not quarters. A short horizon isn't a lack of ambition; it's a bet that we can't see clearly much further out than that, so committing in detail past it is just guessing with extra confidence.

Inside a cycle, the unit is a small batch: a piece of work you can hold in your head and carry to done in that window. If something won't fit, that's information. It means the work is too big and needs cutting into slices, not that the cycle is too short. This is the same instinct that runs through [how we work](/handbook/how-we-work): small things ship, stay reviewable, and keep us close to a working state.

## Plans that survive contact with reality

A good plan is one you can afford to be wrong about. We write plans to be revised, not obeyed. When the work teaches us something the plan didn't know, the plan loses and we update it, out loud, without treating it as a failure.

That's why we keep plans short. A one-paragraph plan is cheap to change when reality argues back; a thirty-page one develops a gravity of its own, and people start defending the document instead of pursuing the outcome. The point of planning isn't the plan. It's the thinking the plan forced, and thinking is allowed to change its mind.

<Callout type="note" title="Re-planning is not failing">
  Changing the plan when the facts change is the plan working, not the plan
  breaking. The only real failure is following a plan you already know is wrong
  because changing it would feel like admitting something.
</Callout>

## No sprint dogma

We borrow what's useful from how teams organize work and leave the rest. Short cycles: yes. A ritual for every occasion, points, velocity charts, a ceremony to plan the meeting about the planning: no. Every one of those exists to solve a problem, and if we don't have the problem, importing the ceremony just taxes us to look like a "real" team.

We stay suspicious of process that arrives by default. If a planning habit isn't paying for itself, we say so and drop it. Cadence should feel like a rhythm that helps you know what's next, not a set of hoops you clear on a schedule. When a ritual becomes the point instead of the work, it's gone.

## Pacing over pressure

Pace matters more than speed. A team that sprints flat out burns down, ships worse, and can't sustain the one thing that actually compounds: showing up steadily, cycle after cycle, for a long time. We'd rather move at a pace we can hold indefinitely than spike and crash.

Practically, that means we don't overfill a cycle to look busy, and we leave slack for the things planning can't foresee: the bug that surfaces, the good idea that lands mid-cycle, the day someone just needs off. A plan packed to the last hour isn't ambitious, it's fragile, and it turns every surprise into a crisis.

## How this connects to deciding

Planning and deciding are close cousins, and they follow the same rules. A plan is a stack of small decisions about what to do next and in what order, and like every decision here it has an owner, gets made in the open, and can be revisited when the facts change. For the mechanics of who decides and how, see [decisions](/handbook/decisions). Planning is just deciding, laid out over the next couple of weeks.

docs.title: How we review PRs
docs.description: The mechanical checklist for getting a pull request reviewed and merged here. The why behind it lives in how we review code; this is the how.
docs.body:
[How we review code](/handbook/code-review) is about the spirit of review: kind, rigorous, aimed at the reader a year out. This page is the mechanical companion, the actual checklist for opening a pull request, reviewing one, and merging it. If the two ever seem to disagree, the spirit wins; this is just the routine that serves it.

## Before you ask for review

The author controls most of what makes a review fast. Before you request one:

- **Keep it small and focused.** One change per PR. If it does three things, it's three PRs. A change someone can review in ten minutes gets reviewed in ten minutes.
- **Review your own diff first.** Read every line as if it were someone else's. You'll catch the debug print and the stray file before a human spends attention on them.
- **Write the description for the reviewer.** What it does, and more usefully why. Link the issue. Call out the risky part and anything you're unsure about; pointing at your own soft spot gets you a better review, not a worse grade.
- **Separate the noise.** Put a rename or a formatting pass in its own commit, or its own PR, so the reviewer isn't hunting for the real change in a wall of diff.
- **Get CI green.** Don't ask a person to review what the machine hasn't checked. Open a draft PR if you want early eyes before it's finished.

## Who reviews, and how fast

Anyone competent in the area can review; you don't need a specific senior name on it. One thoughtful approval is enough for most changes. Pull in a second reviewer yourself when the change is risky, touches a security or data boundary, or you just want another set of eyes.

Reviewing is real work, not an interruption to get to later. Small PRs deserve a fast turnaround, ideally same day. If you can't give a change the attention it needs right now, say so instead of rubber-stamping it; a fast approval on code nobody read is how the 2am page gets written.

## The reviewer's checklist

Read it like you'll maintain it, because you might. Concretely:

- Does it actually do what the description says?
- What about the edge the author probably didn't hit: the empty list, the second org, the retry, the timeout?
- What's the call site you can't see in this diff? Does this break a caller?
- Is it clear? Naming, a comment that explains the why, an abstraction no cleverer than the problem.
- Are there [tests where they earn their keep](/handbook/testing), and do they test behavior rather than restate the code?
- Did the things that travel with the change travel: the docs, the OpenAPI-facing bits, the [customer heads-up](/handbook/customer-comms) if it's breaking?

<Callout type="brand">
  Mark what's blocking and what isn't. Prefix the optional stuff ("nit:", "idea:") so the author knows what must change before merge and what's just a thought. A review where everything reads as mandatory is exhausting and slow.
</Callout>

## Merging

The author merges, once there's an approval and CI is green. Squash the noisy commits so the history reads as one coherent change. The moment it lands on `main` it's on its way to production, so if you wouldn't want it deployed right now, it isn't ready; the rest of that story is in [shipping and releasing](/handbook/shipping-and-releasing).

## Disagreement

You'll disagree sometimes, and that's the point of review, not a failure of it. Argue it in the open, briefly, on the merits. Most disagreements dissolve once both people say what they actually mean. When one doesn't, the author usually gets the call on reversible things since they [own what they ship](/handbook/feature-ownership), and you pull in a third person for the genuinely hard, expensive ones.
