We disagree a fair amount, on purpose. A team that never argues is either not paying attention or not being honest. The goal isn't to avoid conflict, it's to have it well: out in the open, aimed at the problem, and resolved without anyone carrying a grudge home. This is the lightweight path for getting there.

## Assume good intent

Start from the belief that the other person is smart, cares about the same outcome you do, and has a reason for their position that you can't see yet. Almost every disagreement here is two people who both want the thing to be good and picture "good" a little differently.

That assumption changes how the conversation goes. "Why would you do it that way?" as a real question gets you somewhere. As an accusation it gets you a defensive standoff. Same words, different fight.

## Talk to the person, directly and first

If something's bothering you about someone's work or a call they made, take it to them, not around them. Directly, and before it grows. A quiet word early is a five-minute fix. The same thing left to simmer, or aired to everyone except the person involved, turns into a thing that needs a meeting.

This is just [feedback](/handbook/feedback) pointed at a disagreement. Say the specific thing, say it kindly, say it to their face. Most disagreements end right here, two people talking, and never need anything more.

<Callout type="note" title="Directly doesn't mean privately">
  Direct means to the person, not necessarily in a DM. A lot of good
  disagreement happens right in the open thread where the decision lives, and
  that's healthy. See [decisions](/handbook/decisions).
</Callout>

## Disagree, then commit

This is the part that keeps a small team moving. You get to argue hard for your position, right up until a decision is made. Once it's made, you commit to it, fully, even if it wasn't your pick. No relitigating it in the hallway, no quiet sandbagging, no "well, I said so" when it wobbles.

Disagree-and-commit only works if the disagreeing was real. So say your piece plainly while the question's still open. Bring your best argument. Then, when the call goes another way, get behind it like it was yours. You backed the process even when you didn't get the outcome, and that's worth more than being right.

If it turns out the decision was wrong, that's fine too. We change our minds when reality tells us to. Committing to a call isn't a vow to defend it forever, it's a promise not to undermine it while it's the plan. Read [how we decide](/handbook/decisions) for how the call gets made and revisited.

## When to pull in a third person

Most of the time you won't need to. But if you and someone else are genuinely stuck, going in circles, or it's gotten personal enough that neither of you is hearing the other, bring in a third person. Not to referee and declare a winner, but to add context, ask the question you're both missing, or just break the loop.

Pick someone you both trust and keep it in the open where you can. The goal is to get unstuck, not to build a case. And pulling someone in early, before it curdles, is a sign of good judgment, not a failure to handle your own business.

## Disagreement in the open is a feature

None of this is damage control. Healthy disagreement, done in public, is one of the ways we get to good answers. It means people care, they're paying attention, and they trust each other enough to push. A team where everyone nods along is a team that's about to walk off a cliff together.

So argue well. Assume the best of each other, keep it about the work, commit once it's settled, and let people see you do it. That's the method, and it's most of [how we work](/handbook/how-we-work).

docs.title: Security and trust
docs.description: How we think about security, privacy, and earning the trust people place in us.
docs.body:
People trust us with their data and their systems. That trust is slow to earn and fast to lose, and no amount of good marketing survives one careless breach. So we treat security and privacy as part of building the product, not a compliance chore we bolt on later. This page is our stance, so you can hold us to it.

## Secure by default

The secure path has to be the easy path, or it won't get taken. We build so that the default configuration is the safe one, and doing the risky thing takes deliberate effort and a good reason. Secrets stay out of the code and out of the logs. Data is encrypted in transit and at rest as a matter of course, not as a feature we remember to turn on. If security depends on every engineer remembering to do the careful thing every single time, it will fail, so we push it into the defaults where it holds up on its own.

## Least privilege

Access is granted narrowly and reviewed often. People, and systems, get exactly the permissions the job requires and nothing spare, because every extra grant is a bigger blast radius when something goes wrong. This applies to us as much as anyone: standing access to production and to customer data is kept tight, logged, and revisited, not handed out broadly for convenience and forgotten.

## Collect the minimum

The safest data is the data you never collected. We ask for the minimum we actually need to make the product work, and we're skeptical of collecting anything "just in case." Data we don't hold can't leak, can't be subpoenaed, and can't be misused. When we do collect something, we're clear about why, and we don't quietly repurpose it later for something you didn't sign up for.

## Honest, fast incident handling

<Callout type="warn" title="When something goes wrong">
  We tell you promptly and truthfully. No downplaying, no burying it in a quarterly footnote, no waiting until we're sure nobody noticed.
</Callout>

Something will eventually go wrong; it does for everyone. What separates trustworthy from not is what happens next. We handle incidents fast and honestly: contain it, fix it, figure out how it happened, and tell the people affected in plain language and without delay. The postmortem is blameless, because the goal is a system that doesn't fail that way again, not a person to point at. It's the same posture we take with [engineering incidents](/handbook/incidents), and we hold to it even when the truth is embarrassing. Especially then.

## Responsible disclosure welcome

If you've found a vulnerability in something we run, we want to hear about it, and we'll treat you like an ally, not a threat. Email us at [hey@flagon.io](mailto:hey@flagon.io) with what you found and how to reproduce it. We'll acknowledge it, work the fix, and credit you if you'd like. Good-faith security research makes our product safer, and researchers who take the time to tell us instead of selling it deserve a thank-you and a straight answer, not a lawyer.

## Transparent, even when it's uncomfortable

We [build in the open](/handbook/open-source), and that shapes how we do security. It doesn't mean publishing secrets; it means being honest about how the system works, what we collect, and where we've fallen short. When we get something wrong, we'd rather say so than hope nobody looks. Transparency you only offer when the news is good isn't transparency, it's public relations, and people can tell the difference.

## Certifications, when they're earned

We claim a certification only when we've earned it, and not a day before. The security itself is real today: the practices on this page are how we operate now, not aspirations. Formal attestations like SOC 2 are ones we pursue and pass as we grow into them, and when we pass an audit we'll say so, with the report to back it up. We won't put a logo on the site for one we haven't. Judge us on the practices, which are real, not on a plaque.

The short version: we protect your data like it's ours, we tell you the truth when things go sideways, and we earn the trust the slow, honest way.

docs.title: Share options
docs.description: Everyone here gets equity. This is how our option grants work: the terms, the vesting, and the plain-English answers to the questions everyone has.
headings: What are my options actually worth?
What happens to my options if I leave?
Someone messaged me offering to buy my Flagon shares. Should I?
Can I suggest changes to my option agreement?
How do I keep track of all this?
docs.body:
We want everyone building Flagon to own a real piece of it. If this works, the people who made it work should share in what they built, not just watch someone else cash out. So equity isn't a perk reserved for executives here. Everyone gets a meaningful option grant as part of their [compensation](/handbook/compensation), on terms we've deliberately made as team-friendly as we can.

This page explains how that works in plain language. It is not tax or legal advice: equity is genuinely individual, so for anything specific to your situation, talk to your own accountant. We'll help you find one if you need.

## The terms, up front

- **A real grant, for everyone.** As part of your offer you receive an option to buy stock in the company. Roughly how much is set by your [level](/handbook/compensation), the same framework we use for salary, so it isn't a negotiation.
- **Four-year vesting, one-year cliff.** You vest 25% after your first year, then monthly over the following three years, fully vested at four. Vesting starts on your **start date**, not after some "probation period."
- **A ten-year window to exercise.** If you leave, you have ten years from the grant date to exercise your vested options. The industry standard is a brutal 90 days, which quietly forces people to either find a lot of cash fast or walk away from what they earned. We think that's mean, so we don't do it.
- **Double-trigger acceleration.** If Flagon is ever acquired and you're let go in connection with that, your unvested options vest immediately. This protection is usually reserved for executives; we extend it to everyone, because it's the fair version.
- **You only lose vested options for genuine cause.** Resigning, being let go for performance, redundancy: in all of these you keep every option you've vested. Only real misconduct (fraud, material harm to the company) forfeits vested equity.

## The questions everyone actually has

### What is a stock option?

It's the right to buy shares in Flagon at a fixed price (the "strike price" or "exercise price") set on the day it's granted, no matter what the shares are worth later. If the company grows and the shares become worth more than your strike price, that difference is yours. "Exercising" just means choosing to buy those shares at that fixed price.

### What does vesting mean?

You don't get the whole grant on day one, otherwise someone could join for a week and walk away with a chunk of the company. Instead it's earned over four years on the schedule above. Vesting starts your first day.

### What are my options actually worth?

Honestly? Nobody can tell you for certain, and anyone who claims to is selling something. The shares are private and illiquid, so there's no live market price. We can tell you the strike price and the most recent formal valuation, but that's a snapshot, not a promise. Equity is real upside if the company does well and worth nothing if it doesn't, and we'd rather say that plainly than dress it up.

### What happens to my options if I leave?

You keep everything you've vested, and you have ten years from the grant date to exercise it. Vesting stops the day you leave, but nothing you've already earned disappears. The only exception is being let go for genuine cause, as above.

### Are there tax implications?

Yes, and they depend heavily on where you are and what you do, which is exactly why we can't advise you on them. Exercising and selling options can each trigger tax. Where we're able to, we grant options in the most tax-advantaged form your jurisdiction allows, but the rules are individual. Before you exercise anything, talk to a tax advisor. This is the one place where "just wing it" can cost you real money.

### Someone messaged me offering to buy my Flagon shares. Should I?

No. Don't engage. Our shares can't be transferred without board approval, so any deal a random platform or cold DM offers you simply isn't valid, no matter how it's dressed up. If there's ever a legitimate way to sell some of your equity, it will come directly from us, announced to the whole team at once, never from a LinkedIn ad. If you're approached and unsure, ask us in the open.

### Can I suggest changes to my option agreement?

Generally no, and that's on purpose. We use one standard set of agreements for everyone, pre-approved and consistent, so nobody gets a secretly better or worse deal than the person next to them. The trade is that the standard terms are already written to be as team-friendly as we could make them. If you spot an actual error in your paperwork, of course tell us.

### How do I keep track of all this?

Your grants, vesting, strike price, and what it would cost to exercise all live in the cap-table tool we use, signed in with your Flagon email. You'll always be able to see exactly where you stand.

<Callout type="brand" title="The deal we'd want ourselves">
  We designed the equity terms to be the version we'd want if the roles were
  reversed: everyone included, a long window to exercise, protection if we're
  acquired, and nothing clawed back for leaving on normal terms. If any of that
  ever stops being true, it's a bug worth raising.
</Callout>

Still have a question this doesn't answer? Ask in the open, in [Discord](https://discord.gg/dtYQs6rPXN) or at [hey@flagon.io](mailto:hey@flagon.io), and we'll add the answer here.

docs.title: Shipping and releasing
docs.description: How a change actually gets to production here: small pull requests, a trunk that's always releasable, and deploys boring enough to do on a Friday.
headings: Ship behind a flag when it's not ready to be seen
Continuous for the services, deliberate for what others depend on
docs.body:
This is the mechanical companion to [how we build](/handbook/how-we-build): not the philosophy of shipping small, but what the path from your machine to production actually looks like. The whole thing is designed so that releasing is uneventful. A release that makes anyone nervous is a bug in the process.

## The path a change takes

1. **Branch off `main`.** Keep the change small and focused. If it's growing arms and legs, that's a signal to split it, not to push on.
2. **Open a pull request.** Describe what it does and, more usefully, why. Draft it early if you want eyes before it's finished.
3. **Get it reviewed.** Small changes get fast, real reviews; that's the deal in [how we review code](/handbook/code-review), and the step-by-step is in [how we review PRs](/handbook/how-we-review-prs). Keep the noisy commits (a rename, a formatting pass) separate from the substantive one so the reviewer isn't hunting for signal.
4. **Merge to `main`.** CI runs the [tests](/handbook/testing) and, when it's green, deploys both services automatically: the app to Vercel and the API to Fly. There's no separate "release" ceremony to schedule.

## Main stays releasable, always

`main` should be deployable at any moment, not after someone finishes one more fix. This is the single rule that makes everything else work: when the trunk is always green, shipping is routine and a release is a non-event. If `main` isn't releasable, fixing that is the most important thing in the building until it is.

<Callout type="brand">
  If you'd be uncomfortable with `main` deploying to production by accident right now, it isn't ready. Get it back to green before you do anything else.
</Callout>

## Ship behind a flag when it's not ready to be seen

A change being merged and a feature being visible are two different events, and it's often right to separate them. Merge the code early, in small pieces, with the new behavior gated off. Then turn it on for yourself, then for a few friendly users, then for everyone, watching as you widen the circle. This is what lets us [ship the smallest useful change](/handbook/iteration) without waiting for a whole feature to be finished before any of it lands.

It also means a bad release is a config change to reverse, not a frantic rollback.

## Continuous for the services, deliberate for what others depend on

The app and the API deploy continuously on every merge to `main`, because we own both ends and can fix forward fast. The things other people build against are different. The [public API](/handbook/tech-stack) is a contract: a breaking change gets versioned and announced, not slipped out, which is the whole point of [customer comms as an engineer](/handbook/customer-comms). The public SDKs and client CLI [on the roadmap](/roadmap) will release the same way when they land: a tagged version, a changelog entry a human can actually read, and semver that means what it says. Breaking someone's build to save yourself a few minutes of care is not a trade we make.

## When a release goes wrong

It will, sometimes. The response is calm and practiced: flip the flag off or roll forward with a fix, get users back to working, and only then figure out what happened. The full playbook, including the blameless write-up afterward, is in [when things break](/handbook/incidents). The goal is never to find who to blame. It's to make the system a little harder to break the same way twice.

docs.title: Side gigs
docs.description: Our stance on side projects, moonlighting, and who owns what you build on your own time.
headings: Money on the side is fine
docs.body:
We hire builders, and builders build. A lot of the best people we know have a side project or two going, and we take that as a good sign, not a threat. Pre-existing open-source work is one of the strongest signals we look for, precisely because it means someone finds the craft fun rather than a chore. So the default here is simple: your time outside work is yours, and we're glad when you spend some of it making things.

## Money on the side is fine

Some of those projects earn money, and that's genuinely fine. We call them side gigs on purpose, because that's what they are: a thing on the side, not the main event.

The one line that matters: Flagon needs to be your main focus while you're here. We're small, and that only works if the people building it are actually invested in it, not treating it as a paycheck that funds the real thing. So a few hours a week on a paid side project is no problem; a second full-time job wearing a disguise is. If a side gig starts pulling on the time or attention the work needs, that's the signal to rebalance, and we'd rather talk about it early than pretend it isn't happening.

If your side thing is growing into something you'd want to do full-time one day, tell us. That's not a betrayal, it's useful information, and we'd rather help you plan the runway than be surprised by a resignation. [Playing the long game](/handbook/values#the-long-game) with people means their goals and ours don't have to be secret from each other.

## Who owns what you make

Fuzziness here causes real headaches, so the lines are simple:

- **What you build on your own time, with your own tools, is yours.** We don't try to claim ownership of personal projects, open-source contributions, or anything else you make outside the work. Go build.
- **What you build for Flagon belongs to Flagon.** Normal, and the reason your pay and equity exist.
- **Don't cross the streams.** The one thing to be careful about is mixing Flagon's non-open code or confidential context into a personal project, or vice versa. Anything of ours that's explicitly open source is fair to use; anything that isn't, keep out of your side work. When in doubt, ask before you entangle them, because untangling it later is where the genuine legal headaches live.

<Callout type="note" title="Use your judgement, and just ask">
  None of this is meant to police your weekends. If something feels like a grey
  area, a competing product, a client who's also our customer, unusual time
  demands, raise it in the open early. A two-minute conversation beats a
  conflict nobody named.
</Callout>

docs.title: Spending money
docs.description: How we handle company spending: trust-based, with judgment and documentation instead of an approval gauntlet.
docs.body:
You'll spend company money often, and we want that to be easy. Flagon runs lean, because the less we waste the more runway we have to make this work; see [staying alive](/handbook/staying-alive). But being productive and effective matters more than saving a few dollars. This page exists to help you make good calls, not to make you fill in a form.

## Guiding principles

We run a context-based expense policy rather than an approval-based one. Before you spend, ask yourself two questions:

- Can you clearly explain why this expense is in Flagon's best interest?
- Would you be comfortable explaining it to the whole team, in public?

If the answer to both is **yes**, it's almost certainly fine. If you find yourself inventing a justification, you already have your answer. When you genuinely aren't sure, ask for **context, not permission**: a quick question in the open beats either a rubber-stamp or a guess.

## How it works

- **Use the company card for work expenses,** not your personal one. If you ever have to use a personal card by accident, claim it back promptly with a receipt.
- **Small and obviously work-related?** Just buy it and note what it was. A subscription you need, a book, cloud credits, a domain. No permission needed.
- **Bigger or less obvious?** Say what and why in the open first, so someone can catch the thing you didn't think of. That's a sanity check, not a gate.
- **Recurring costs are small forever-decisions.** Before adding a subscription, check we don't already pay for something that does the job. See [adding tools](/handbook/adding-tools).

## Documentation, and why it matters

A trust-based policy only survives if everyone keeps the paperwork clean. Attach an itemized receipt and a short memo to anything past a small threshold, promptly, while you still remember what it was for. A good memo says what the item was, why the business needed it, and any useful context: who it was for, which project. An itemized receipt plus that memo is all finance or an auditor should need to understand a charge months later.

Missing receipts and vague memos turn into hours of "what was this charge from June?" at audit time. A quick upload now saves everyone that later. If documentation consistently slips, the only alternatives are rigid pre-approvals for everyone or treating it as a performance issue, and we'd much rather not go there.

## What's reasonable to spend on

- **Equipment.** A machine that doesn't fight you, a decent monitor, and a chair that doesn't wreck your back are all easy yeses. Refurbished is often great value. We tend to centralize laptop purchases so they're tracked properly and can be returned or passed on when someone leaves.
- **Software.** Individual tools are your preference, and we love a good recommendation. We're deliberately wary of adding *collaborative* software, since each new shared tool is another place the truth can fragment; the reasoning is in [adding tools](/handbook/adding-tools).
- **Learning.** Books, courses, a conference that makes you better at the work. Growing at the job is part of the job, see [growing here](/handbook/growing-here).
- **Travel and working together.** Economy by default, and we actively encourage working in person when it's useful. If you're in the same place as colleagues, a shared meal is on the company.

## When spending isn't okay

Some things are clearly not company expenses: personal purchases on the company card, or anything you wouldn't be comfortable explaining publicly. If a questionable expense was an honest misunderstanding, we'll just clarify and move on. Deliberately spending company money in ways that aren't in Flagon's interest, or trying to route around the guidelines, is a different thing, and we treat it as [serious misconduct](/handbook/how-we-part-ways).

## Bigger vendor contracts

Some spend isn't a personal subscription but a platform a team runs, on a contract that bills continuously and can reach real money, think infrastructure or security tooling. The guiding principles above still apply; they just matter more. Whoever has the most context on the contract owns keeping an eye on usage against its limits so nobody is surprised by the bill, and flags early, before an overage lands and keeps landing, rather than after. Loop in the relevant people (and legal, for anything new) while it's still cheap to change course. Renewals get the same care as a new purchase: do the diligence, don't rubber-stamp.

docs.title: Staying alive
docs.description: Financial discipline and honesty, and why staying independent is what lets us keep our promises.
headings: We spend like the money is real, because it is
docs.body:
Everything else in this handbook, the craft, the values, the promises, depends on Flagon still being here to keep them. A company that runs out of money keeps none of them. That makes financial discipline the thing that protects everything else, and this page is how we think about it.

## Default alive

There are two states a company can be in. Default alive means that on its current trajectory, with what it's making and what it's spending, it survives without needing anyone to rescue it. Default dead means it's counting on something that hasn't happened yet: a raise, a deal, a miracle. We intend to be the first kind, on purpose, as a standing condition and not a lucky accident.

Being default alive is what buys us the freedom the rest of this handbook assumes. It's how we can say no to money that would cost us our [values](/handbook/values), turn down a bad deal, or hold a fair price when a greedier one was available. You can only keep those promises if you're not desperate. Discipline now is what makes principle possible later.

## We spend like the money is real, because it is

Every dollar Flagon spends is a dollar a customer handed us on the assumption we'd use it well. We treat it that way: not cheap for its own sake, just deliberate, weighing whether a thing is worth it the way you would with your own money, because it is our own money. How that plays out line by line lives on [how we spend money](/handbook/spending-money).

## We don't buy status

A lot of company spending isn't about getting something done. It's about looking a certain way: the impressive office nobody needed, the tools bought to seem serious, the headcount added to look bigger in a meeting. It's status dressed up as necessity, and it's how small companies quietly bleed out while feeling successful.

We skip it. We'd rather look smaller than we are and have money in the bank than look impressive and be one bad quarter from trouble. Nobody who matters is fooled by the pageantry anyway, and the people paying for it are always the customers. Frugality here isn't self-denial, it's respect: for the money, and for the people who trusted us with it.

## Independence

Staying disciplined is what keeps us independent, and independence is what lets us keep our word. The moment a company depends on someone, an investor who wants a quick return, a single customer who can dictate terms, next month's rescue, its promises get negotiable. It starts making decisions to please whoever holds the leverage instead of whoever it's supposed to serve. We've watched good companies get quietly rewritten this way, one reasonable-sounding compromise at a time.

Being default alive keeps the leverage on our side. It ties directly to [how we make money](/handbook/how-we-make-money): revenue from happy customers, priced fairly, is money that doesn't come with strings. It's also [the long game](/handbook/values#the-long-game) in its most literal form: the first requirement for being here in ten years is not going broke in the next one.

## Honesty about the numbers

We won't put specific figures on this page, because a stance should outlast any given month's balance. But internally, we don't lie to ourselves about the money, and we don't dress up a bad month as a good one. A company that fools itself about its finances is a company writing its own ending. The whole discipline starts with looking at the real numbers and telling yourself the truth about them.

docs.title: Staying human at a distance
docs.description: Remote kills the hallway, so we rebuild connection on purpose, without forcing fun.
headings: The hallway doesn't come free anymore
docs.body:
Remote work is worth it. But it takes something real, and pretending otherwise is how remote teams end up as a group of strangers who happen to share a repo. The thing it takes is the hallway. In an office, connection is a byproduct: you bump into people, overhear a joke, get coffee, learn that the person three desks over is a person. Remote deletes all of that by default, so we put it back deliberately. Doing it deliberately is the part that matters.

## The hallway doesn't come free anymore

In an office you'd have to actively work to avoid ever talking to a colleague as a human. Remote flips the effort: now you have to actively work to talk to one. Left alone, remote optimizes ruthlessly for tasks. Every interaction becomes a ticket, a review, a thread with a purpose, and the low-stakes human stuff that makes a team feel like a team never happens, because nothing schedules it.

That's not a people problem or a culture problem. It's a structural fact about the medium, and the fix is structural too: if connection won't happen by accident, we make a little room for it to happen on purpose. Not a lot. Just enough.

## What we actually do

A few deliberate, low-pressure things. All optional, none of them mandatory fun:

- **Coffee chats.** A short, no-agenda call with someone, sometimes randomly paired, sometimes because you've been meaning to. The rule is there's no rule: talk about the work, or don't. The point is to know the person behind the pull requests.
- **Show-and-tell.** A standing, casual slot to show something you made, a thing you learned, a side project, a rabbit hole you fell down. Half of team culture is just watching each other be curious out loud.
- **A channel for none of it.** A place that is explicitly not about work: the dog, the terrible weather, the thing you're cooking, the game you can't stop playing. It sounds trivial. It's load-bearing.
- **Celebrating wins, out loud.** When something ships or someone pulls off something hard, we say so where everyone can see it. Remote makes wins easy to miss, because there's no room that spontaneously claps. So we clap on purpose.

<Callout type="brand" title="No mandatory fun">
  Everything here is an invitation, not attendance. The fastest way to kill
  real connection is to require it and put it on a calendar with a mandatory
  flag. Forced fun isn't fun, it's a meeting wearing a party hat. Show up
  because you want to, skip it when you don't, and no one's counting.
</Callout>

## Where it gets hard

This is harder at our size, not easier. A big company can spin up a dozen affinity groups and a full-time culture team. We can't, and won't pretend to. When the crew is small, one person having a rough month or just being heads-down is enough for a couple of these rituals to quietly go quiet. There's no crowd to carry the energy. It takes real individual effort, from people who'd often rather just keep working.

We think that effort is worth it, and we'd rather admit it's effort than sell you a frictionless "culture" that runs itself. It doesn't. Someone has to start the coffee chat, post in the not-work channel first, notice the win and say it out loud. Sometimes that someone is you, and the small act of starting it is most of the job.

The payoff is a team you'd actually want to work with for years, one where directness lands as care instead of coldness, because you know the person on the other end. A lot of this handbook depends on that: the [async](/handbook/working-async) distance, the blunt [feedback](/handbook/feedback), the [communication](/handbook/communication) norms. None of it survives between strangers. So we keep the strangers from forming, one slightly awkward hallway moment at a time.

docs.title: Staying secure
docs.description: Security is everyone's job, not just engineering's. The basic habits we all keep so one careless moment doesn't become a breach.
docs.body:
The most common way into a company isn't clever code, it's a reused password or a convincing email. Security here isn't only an engineering concern (the product and code side lives in [security](/handbook/security)); it's a set of habits everyone keeps. The weakest link is usually a real person having a distracted day, and that could be any of us. That's why the basics below aren't optional.

## The basics

- **A password manager, and a unique strong password for everything.** No reuse, ever. This one habit shuts the most common door.
- **Two-factor auth on everything that offers it,** ideally an app or a hardware key rather than SMS.
- **Keep your devices locked, encrypted, and up to date.** Updates are boring and they're also how most holes get closed.
- **Least access.** You get access to what the work needs, you ask when you need more, and we take it away when you don't. Standing access you're not using is just risk sitting around.

## Phishing and social engineering

Assume someone will eventually try to trick you, because eventually someone will. Be suspicious of manufactured urgency ("do this right now or else"), of unexpected links and attachments, and of anyone asking you to move money, hand over a credential, or read back a code. When something feels off, slow down and check in the open. Reporting a suspicious message is never overreacting; we'd rather see ten false alarms than miss the one real one.

## Handling data and secrets

- **Customer data is a responsibility, not a resource.** Touch it only when the work genuinely needs it, don't copy it around, and don't paste it into random tools.
- **Secrets never go in code, chat, or a doc.** Keys, tokens, and credentials belong in proper secret storage. If one leaks, rotate it immediately and say so. A leaked secret caught and rotated fast is a non-event; one quietly hidden is how a breach starts.

## If something goes wrong

If you think you clicked the wrong thing, leaked a credential, or lost a device, tell us immediately and in the open, however embarrassing it feels. There is zero blame for reporting fast, and it is the single most useful thing you can do. The only unforgivable move is going quiet and hoping it's fine. A quick heads-up usually turns a scare into a shrug; [incidents](/handbook/incidents) covers what happens from there.

docs.title: Support and customer care
docs.description: Support is craft, not a cost center. Here's how we treat the people who use what we make.
headings: The people who build it help support it
Fast and honest beats polished and slow
Every support conversation is a signal
docs.body:
How you treat people when something goes wrong tells them more about you than anything you say when it's going right. Support is where that happens, and we refuse to treat it as a cost to minimize. It's craft, same as the code and the design, and it's one of the clearest places our values show up or don't.

## The people who build it help support it

We don't build a wall between the people who make the thing and the people who answer for it. The person who wrote the code is often the person who can actually fix your problem, and putting them within earshot of the people hitting it keeps everyone honest. It's harder to ship a confusing thing when you're the one explaining it at the other end.

This is the same instinct as [how we build](/handbook/how-we-build): you own what you ship, and owning it doesn't stop at deploy. Support isn't a department that catches what engineering throws over the wall. It's part of owning the work all the way through.

## Fast and honest beats polished and slow

When you're stuck, a quick honest answer is worth ten slow polished ones. So we aim to reply fast, say what we actually know, and not hide behind a script. If it's a bug, we say it's a bug. If we don't know yet, we say that too, and we say when we'll know more. If we broke it, we own it instead of reaching for the passive voice.

People can tell the difference between a real person working the problem and a form letter buying time. We'd rather be the first thing, even when the honest answer is "you've found a rough edge and we haven't fixed it yet."

<Callout type="note" title="The tone we're after">
  Talk to people the way you'd want a sharp friend to talk to you when you're
  stuck: direct, warm, no runaround, and never pretending the problem is smaller
  than it is.
</Callout>

## Every support conversation is a signal

A support ticket isn't just a thing to close. It's the product telling you where it's confusing, where it breaks, where the docs went quiet exactly when someone needed them. The same question three times isn't three tickets; it's one thing to fix. We treat the pattern in what people ask as a roadmap, and the best outcome of a support conversation is often a change that means nobody has to ask again.

That's why support living close to the people who build matters. The signal is worth the most when it reaches someone who can act on it, before it gets flattened into a number on a dashboard.

## Never make someone feel stupid

Nobody hits a rough edge on purpose. When someone's confused, that's usually the product's failure to be clear, not the person's failure to be smart, and we answer like we believe that. No condescension, no "as stated in the docs," no making a person feel small for not knowing the thing we never explained well.

Being warm here isn't softness; it's respect, and it's part of our [values](/handbook/values). The people who use what we make are trusting us with their time and their work. Treating a support conversation as a chance to earn that trust, rather than a ticket to clear, is the whole point. If someone walks away from a rough moment feeling respected, we did the job right, even on a day the product let them down.

docs.title: Team changes
docs.description: How people move between teams and change what they own here: low ceremony, in the open, and without drama.
headings: Wanting to work on something else
When the company initiates a change
docs.body:
Nobody here is bolted to one team forever. What you work on can change as you grow, as your interests shift, or as the company's needs move, and we try to make that change low-friction and free of the usual politics. A company that makes internal moves painful just teaches its best people to change companies instead of teams.

## Wanting to work on something else

If you're drawn to different work, say so early and in the open. Talk to your current [manager](/handbook/how-we-manage) and to whoever leads the area you're eyeing. It's a conversation, not a petition you have to win, and raising it is not disloyal. We would much rather help you find the work that fits than watch you quietly check out, or start interviewing elsewhere, because you assumed the answer was no.

## How a move actually happens

- **Talk it through in the open,** with both teams, not as a back-room deal.
- **Hand off cleanly.** A move should never drop a ball. What you own now gets transferred deliberately, with the context written down, so nothing quietly breaks after you've moved on. This is [owning the whole outcome](/handbook/operating-principles) applied to leaving a team, not just joining one.
- **Time it so both sides are okay.** Not instant if you're mid-something critical, but not blocked indefinitely either. Most moves can be staged over a few weeks.
- **Write the change down.** Update where it's recorded so the org stays legible and the next person isn't confused about who owns what.

## Changing role or scope

Growing into a bigger role, or a different kind of work, follows the same instinct. Taking on management is the clearest example: it's a move into a [different kind of work](/handbook/how-we-manage), decided in the open, not a rung you climb by seniority. Scope changes are about the work you're trusted to own, and they show up in your [level and pay](/handbook/compensation) through the same framework as everyone else's, see [growing here](/handbook/growing-here).

## When the company initiates a change

Sometimes it's the work that needs to move, not a person's preference. When we reshape a team, we do it transparently and explain the reasoning, the same way we make any other [decision](/handbook/decisions). The shape of the org follows the problems worth solving, see [small by design](/handbook/how-were-structured). What we don't do is a surprise reorg dropped from above with no context; if the structure is changing, you'll hear why.

<Callout type="brand" title="Moving on isn't a betrayal">
  Whether it's a move between teams or, eventually, a move out of Flagon
  entirely, we'd rather handle it like adults, in the open and with a clean
  handoff, than punish honesty about it. See [how we part
  ways](/handbook/how-we-part-ways) for the same principle at the far end.
</Callout>

docs.title: Tech stack
docs.description: What Flagon is built with, and why: two small, independently deployed services, boring proven tools, and a hard rule that the API is the only thing that owns data.
headings: The app is a thin gateway
How to read this page later
docs.body:
This is what Flagon runs on and the reasoning behind each choice. None of it is exotic. That's the point: we spend our interesting-technology budget on the product, not the plumbing, exactly as [how we build](/handbook/how-we-build) describes. It all lives in one monorepo, [flagon-io/flagon](https://github.com/flagon-io/flagon), but it deploys as two separate services that talk to each other over HTTP. They work together; neither is bundled inside the other.

## The two halves

| Piece | Stack | What it is | Hosted on |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `app/` (`app.flagon.io`) | Next.js, TypeScript | the web UI, the gateway, and auth | Vercel |
| `api/` (`api.flagon.io`) | Go (chi + huma) | the source of truth: all data and logic | Fly.io |

Underneath both sits **Postgres**, and a shared **`@flagon-io/ui`** package holds the components the app is built from. The two services are wired together with a couple of environment variables (`FLAGON_API_URL`, `FLAGON_INTERNAL_TOKEN`), and that's the whole coupling.

## The API owns everything real

`api/` is a Go program built on chi and huma. It's the source of truth: it owns all the business data and logic, it's multi-tenant through Postgres Row-Level Security scoped by `org_id`, and it's the only place that holds real secrets like the database credentials and the Stripe keys. It ships as a single Go binary with its schema migrations embedded, so deploying it is running one file that migrates itself on boot.

Go earns its place here for the same reasons it always does: it compiles to that one static binary with nothing to install around it, the standard library covers most of what we need, and it stays legible to people who didn't write it, which matters for a project we want strangers to [read and contribute to](/handbook/open-source).

<Callout type="brand" title="One rule holds the architecture together">
  The API is the only thing that touches business data or Stripe. If you're reaching around it, stop. That single boundary is what keeps the system honest as it grows.
</Callout>

## The app is a thin gateway

`app/` is a Next.js app in TypeScript, and it's deliberately thin. It renders the UI, it handles authentication (sign-up, login, sessions, email verification), and it forwards everything else to the API. It does not reach into the product's data or talk to Stripe; when it needs something real, it asks the API. Keeping the app thin is what lets the API stay the single source of truth instead of one of two places the rules live.

TypeScript because the types pay for themselves the first time you rename a field, and because we generate a typed client from the API's OpenAPI spec, so the app and the API can't quietly disagree about what an endpoint returns.

## Postgres, and the OpenAPI contract

Everything that persists lives in **Postgres**. In production the two services get their own instances; locally they share one instance with two databases to go easy on a laptop, but the boundary is the same. One store, well understood, that every host already knows how to back up. We reach for a Postgres feature long before we reach for a second piece of infrastructure.

The API is **OpenAPI-first**: every endpoint registered with huma is documented automatically, so the spec can't drift from the code, and the running server serves it live. That spec is the contract the [live API reference](/docs/api) renders from and the typed client is generated against. Public SDKs and a client CLI are [on the roadmap](/roadmap); when they arrive they'll be generated from this same spec rather than hand-written.

## Self-hostable by construction

Because [leaving is always an option](/handbook/open-source), Flagon has to be something you can run yourself. That's two services and a Postgres: point the app at the API with two env vars, give the API a `DATABASE_URL`, and host them wherever you like. Our own instance happens to run on Vercel and Fly, but nothing in the code assumes that.

## How to read this page later

Specific versions and libraries drift, and this page drifts with them rather than listing every dependency; the lock files and `go.mod` are the real answer to "what exactly are we on." What shouldn't drift is the shape: two services, one monorepo, the API owns the data, Postgres underneath. If a proposed change breaks one of those, it needs a good story for why.

docs.title: How we test
docs.description: Tests that earn their keep, catch real regressions, and give you the confidence to ship without slowing everyone down.
headings: tied to behavior, survives a rewrite
tied to implementation, breaks on any refactor
Confidence to ship is the real goal
docs.body:
We test to ship with confidence, not to hit a number. Everything below follows from that. A test suite is a tool, and like any tool it can be sharp and useful or heavy and in the way. We aim for sharp. This is the longer version of the "tests where they earn their keep" line in [how we build](/handbook/how-we-build).

## Tests earn their keep

Every test is code you have to maintain, run, and read. So each one should pay for itself by catching something that would actually hurt. We write tests for the logic that's easy to get subtly wrong, the paths that money and data flow through, and the bugs that have already bitten us once (that last category is non-negotiable: a bug you fixed without a test is a bug you've agreed to ship again).

We don't write tests to make a coverage percentage go up. Coverage tells you what code ran during the suite, not whether it's correct, and chasing the number produces tests that assert nothing while looking diligent. A line can be 100% covered and completely broken.

## Test behavior, not implementation

Test what the code does, not how it does it. A good test reads like a description of a promise the system makes: given this input, you get this result. It should survive a refactor. If you rewrite the internals without changing the behavior and half your tests go red, those tests were pinned to the implementation, and they were costing you the very thing tests are supposed to buy: the freedom to change code safely.

```
# tied to behavior, survives a rewrite
expect(priceFor(cart)).toBe(1200)

# tied to implementation, breaks on any refactor
expect(calc.applyDiscount).toHaveBeenCalledWith(0.1)
```

The second test knows too much. It fails when you rename a method or restructure the math, even when the price is still right, which trains everyone to update tests reflexively instead of trusting them.

## Fast and reliable over exhaustive

A test suite people trust and run is worth more than a thorough one they route around. Two properties matter most.

Fast, because a suite that takes twenty minutes doesn't get run before you push, it gets run by CI after you've moved on. Reliable, because a flaky test is worse than no test: it cries wolf, people learn to hit rerun, and then it's useless the one time it's telling the truth.

<Callout type="warn" title="Flaky tests are a fire, not a chore">
  A test that fails at random is actively eroding trust in the whole suite. Fix it or delete it the day you find it. A quarantined flaky test is a decision to fix it, not a place to forget it.
</Callout>

## What we don't bother testing

Plenty. We generally don't write tests for trivial code with no logic (a getter, a straight passthrough), for third-party libraries (that's their job, not ours), or for throwaway spikes we're about to delete. We lean on types to make whole categories of test unnecessary: if the compiler already guarantees it, a test asserting it is just ceremony. And we don't chase exhaustive tests on the parts of the UI that change every week, where the maintenance cost swamps the payoff.

The heuristic: if a test would only ever fail because someone deliberately changed the behavior it pins, and that behavior doesn't matter, skip it.

## Confidence to ship is the real goal

The question behind every testing decision is: does this let us change the code and release it without holding our breath? That's what keeps `main` releasable and lets us ship small and often. When a test gives you that confidence, keep it. When it just makes the suite slower and the refactor scarier, it's failing at its one job, and you should delete it happily. A leaner suite you believe is worth far more than a bloated one you've learned to ignore.

docs.title: The hiring process
docs.description: The exact stages from first contact to offer, what each one is for, and how long it takes.
docs.body:
[How we hire](/handbook/how-we-hire) covers what we look for and why we run it the way we do. This page is the mechanics: the stages, in order, so you always know where you are and what comes next. There are no hidden rounds and no surprise panels. If a stage below doesn't apply to a particular role, we say so up front rather than adding it just because.

## The stages

**1. You apply, or we reach out.** Either a short application (tell us what you've built and why this role) or a direct message if we came to you. No cover-letter ritual. A link to real work, a repo, a project, a thing you shipped, is worth more than a polished CV.

**2. Intro conversation.** Thirty to forty-five minutes with someone you'd actually work with, not a recruiter reading a script. We talk about what you've made, how you think, and what you want next. It's mutual: you should be sizing us up just as hard, and hard questions are a good sign, not a red flag.

**3. A paid work sample.** Instead of whiteboard puzzles you'll never use again, we pay you to do a small, realistic slice of the actual work, on your own time, usually a few focused hours. You keep the money regardless of the outcome. It's the fairest signal we know: you see what the work is really like, and we see how you think when it's real rather than performed.

**4. Team conversations.** A couple of focused conversations with people you'd work alongside, going deep on how you approach problems, how you work with others, and how you'd fit the way we operate. This is also where you get to interrogate the reality of the job: the good, the annoying, and the still-unfinished.

**5. Decision and offer.** We make up our minds quickly and tell you either way. If it's yes, the offer comes with the math: pay at Flagon is a published [formula](/handbook/compensation), the same for everyone, so the number isn't a negotiation and there's nothing to haggle.

## How long it takes

We aim to move fast, because a slow process is disrespectful of your time and loses good people to companies that got their act together. The target is a couple of weeks from first conversation to decision, faster when we can. If something on our end is going to take longer, we tell you, rather than going quiet.

<Callout type="note" title="You'll never be ghosted">
  At every stage, you get a real answer in a reasonable time. A no comes with a
  reason and comes soon. If you're ever left wondering where things stand, that's
  a bug in our process, and you're welcome to poke us about it.
</Callout>

## How to prepare

Honestly, not much. Bring examples of real work and be ready to talk about the reasoning behind them, not just the result. Come with questions that matter to you, about the work, the money, how decisions get made, whatever you actually need to know to decide. The whole [handbook](/handbook) is fair game, and reading a little of it beforehand tells you more about us than any pitch we could give on a call.

The one thing that helps most: be yourself. We're trying to figure out whether this is a good fit in both directions, and a version of you that's performing for the room makes that harder for everyone.

docs.title: Time off and hours
docs.description: Outcomes over hours, real rest, and playing the long game with your energy.
headings: Async so timezones don't trap you
The long game with your energy
docs.body:
We care about what you make, not how many hours you sat at a desk making it. This page is how we think about time, the working kind and the off kind, and why we treat rest as part of the job rather than a reward for finishing it.

## Hours: outcomes, not clock-watching

There's no timesheet and nobody counting your green dot. We hired you to do good work and to know when it's done, not to perform being busy for eight hours. Some days that's ten hours because you're deep in something and don't want to stop. Some days it's four because the work is finished and the rest is padding.

What matters is that the work is good, that the people who depend on you can, and that you're honest when something's slipping. See [how we work](/handbook/how-we-work) for the mechanics of that. Beyond that, we trust you to run your own day.

## Async so timezones don't trap you

We're [remote-first](/handbook/working-here) and async by default, and a big reason is that we never want your calendar to be hostage to someone else's timezone. You shouldn't have to be awake at 2am for a meeting, and you shouldn't have to live inside a rigid block of "core hours" that happens to suit headquarters, because there is no headquarters. Write things down, let people pick them up when they're awake, and stop treating instant replies as a virtue.

## Real rest, actually taken

"Unlimited PTO" sounds generous and usually isn't. With no number, nobody knows what's okay, so people take less, not more, and the ones who most need a break are the ones who feel guiltiest about it. It quietly turns time off into a thing you have to justify.

We're doing the opposite. We want a sane minimum that people actually take: a real floor, not a vague ceiling. The point of a floor is that it's not optional: you're expected to hit it, and if you're not, that's a problem to fix, not willpower to admire.

<Callout type="brand" title="Rest is not a reward">
  Time off isn't something you earn by burning out first. It's maintenance on
  the person doing the work. We'd rather you take the break before you need it
  than after you've cracked.
</Callout>

How it works: a generous paid floor that we expect you to actually take, plus more whenever you genuinely need it. The specific number lives in your offer, where it's a real commitment rather than a marketing line.

## Sick days are just off

If you're sick, stop working. Rest, get better, come back when you're well. You don't need a doctor's note, you don't need to apologize, and you don't need to half-work through it to prove something. A half-present sick person helps no one and gets everyone else sick. This covers the mind too: a day when your head isn't in it is a fine day to step back.

## The long game with your energy

We're optimizing for still being here, and still enjoying this, years from now. That's one of our [values](/handbook/values), and it applies to people as much as products. Hustle-until-you-break is a bad trade. It looks like speed and it's actually debt: you borrow next month's energy to make this week look busy, and eventually the bill comes due as burnout, sloppy work, and good people leaving.

Sustainable pace isn't the slow option. It's the one that's still shipping good work when the sprinters have quit. Work hard, then genuinely stop. Both parts matter.

docs.title: What we keep private
docs.description: We're public by default, but a few specific things aren't, and each exception has to earn its place.
headings: Secrecy carries the burden of proof
docs.body:
Building in the open is easy to say and harder to mean. We're public by default, genuinely, not as a marketing pose. But "default" is not "always," and pretending otherwise would be its own kind of dishonesty. Here's the actual boundary: what stays private, and why each thing earns its spot on the list.

## The default is open

Start here, because it's the part that's true almost all the time. Decisions, plans, docs, code, arguments, the handbook you're reading: public unless there's a specific reason otherwise. Public channels over DMs, comments over asides, the [GitHub org](https://github.com/flagon-io) over a conversation nobody else can see.

The reason isn't that we're incapable of keeping a secret. It's that openness compounds. Something written in the open is searchable, correctable, and useful to a person you haven't met yet who hits the same wall next month. Every private conversation is a small debt the next person pays.

## What stays private

A short list, and it's meant to stay short:

- **A person's own situation.** Someone's health, family, finances, a hard stretch they're going through: that's theirs to share, at the volume they choose, if at all. It is never ours to broadcast on their behalf.
- **Security fixes before they ship.** When there's a live vulnerability, publishing the details before the patch is out just hands the exploit to whoever's paying attention. We fix quietly, ship, then tell the story afterward. Openness with a delay, not a permanent secret.
- **Things customers trusted us with.** Data, private details, anything shared with us in confidence because they had to in order to use the product. That trust isn't ours to spend on being transparent. It's the whole reason they can rely on us at all.
- **Individual pay.** Not the framework, the individual figures. How we decide pay is public and should be: the bands, the logic, the philosophy. What a specific named person earns is that person's private business, and putting it on blast helps nobody they'd thank you for.

Notice the shape. Two of these are private forever because they belong to someone else (a person's own life, a customer's trust). One is private only until it ships (security). One splits cleanly: the system is public, the individual number isn't.

<Callout type="warn" title="The pay distinction matters">
  "We're transparent about pay" means the method is on the table: anyone can
  read how a number gets reached and argue with it. It does not mean we publish
  a roster of names and salaries. Transparent process, private figures. Those
  are not in tension.
</Callout>

## Secrecy carries the burden of proof

One rule sits under the whole list, and it's the thing to remember if you forget everything else on this page: secrecy has to justify itself. Openness doesn't.

When something's public, that needs no defense; it's the default, and the burden's already met. When you want to keep something private, that's the move that owes an argument. Not a vague "this feels sensitive," but a real one: whose is it to share, who gets hurt if it's out, is this private forever or just private until a patch lands. If you can't answer that, it probably wants to be in the open.

That framing keeps the private list from growing the way private lists always want to grow. Every organization drifts toward keeping more quiet, because in any single moment silence is the low-effort, low-risk choice. Making secrecy carry the burden of proof is how we stop the drift. The list above is short because it has to keep earning its place, item by item, and anything that can't is already public.

None of this is a legal document, and it isn't the fine print on "built in the open." It's the same commitment, told completely enough to include its own exceptions. For how this plays out day to day, see [how we communicate](/handbook/communication) and [how we work](/handbook/how-we-work).

docs.title: Our values
docs.description: The four things we actually mean, what they look like, and what they don't.
docs.body:
Most company values are wall decoration: nouns nobody could argue with, printed nicely, meaning nothing. Ours are supposed to help you decide things when the answer isn't obvious. There are four. Here's what each one means, what it looks like in practice, and the way it goes wrong.

## Make good things

Quality over quantity, always. One thing that's genuinely good beats a pile of features nobody asked for. We'd rather ship less and be proud of it.

**In practice:** you take the extra day to make the thing right instead of shipping the version you'd be embarrassed to demo. You say no to features that would bloat the product. You care about the parts users never see (the error message, the empty state, the thing that happens when the network drops) because that's where good and fine part ways.

**What it does not mean:** polishing forever. "Make good things" is not a license to gold-plate or to never ship. Perfect is a way of not finishing. The bar is good and out the door, not flawless and imaginary. A good thing that shipped beats a great one that didn't.

## Open by default

If we can't explain it in public, that's a signal something's off. The handbook, the roadmap, the reasoning, the misfires: readable by anyone.

**In practice:** you write the decision down where people can see it, not in a DM. You default to the public channel. When you're unsure whether something can be open, the question is "why not?" rather than "why?" This whole handbook is the value in action; see [how this handbook works](/handbook/how-this-handbook-works) for the test we apply.

**What it does not mean:** open with no judgment. Someone's personal situation, an unannounced security fix, private details people trusted us with: those stay closed, obviously. Open by default is a default, not a compulsion to overshare. The point is that secrecy should have to justify itself, not the other way around.

## Built in public

Ship early, listen hard, and let the people using the work shape what comes next. No vaporware, no big reveal.

**In practice:** you put the rough version out and learn from real use instead of guessing behind a curtain for six months. You take the feedback in the [Discord](https://discord.gg/dtYQs6rPXN) seriously. You're comfortable being seen while the work is still in motion, and you let the people using it help shape where it goes next.

**What it does not mean:** shipping junk and calling it transparency. Early isn't an excuse for careless. It still has to be a [good thing](#make-good-things), just an honest, unfinished one. And "built in public" doesn't mean built by committee; we listen hard, then we still decide.

## The long game

No quick exit, no growth-at-all-costs. We're optimizing for still being here, still making useful things, years from now.

**In practice:** you make decisions you won't resent in three years. You don't borrow against the future to make this quarter look good, not with the code, not with the trust, not with people's [energy](/handbook/time-off). You'd rather build something durable slowly than something impressive that collapses.

**What it does not mean:** slow as a personality, or using "long term" to dodge every hard call. The long game is a reason to be decisive now, not an excuse to defer forever. Patience isn't procrastination with better branding.

## Values are behavior, not posters

<Callout type="brand">
  A value you won't act on when it's inconvenient is just a slogan. These count
  when they cost something.
</Callout>

The test for any of these is what happens when it's expensive: when "make good things" means slipping a date, when "open by default" means publishing something awkward, when "the long game" means turning down easy money. That's when they count. We'd rather have four we actually use than twenty we recite. If you catch us not living them, that's a bug; say so, [here](https://github.com/flagon-io) or at [hey@flagon.io](mailto:hey@flagon.io).

docs.title: Visiting customers as an engineer
docs.description: Some things never show up on a call. Sitting next to someone while they use what you built is one of the highest-leverage things an engineer here can do.
docs.body:
We're a [remote company](/handbook/working-async), and most of the time that's exactly right. But there's a specific kind of understanding you only get in the room: watching someone use your product with their real data, their real workflow, and the three other tools they alt-tab to without thinking. People are more candid in person than in any written reply, and the friction that never quite makes it into a support ticket is obvious the moment you see it happen. Going to visit a customer is one of the best uses of an engineer's time we know of, and it's open to you, not just to a sales team.

## Who's worth visiting

The best visits are with customers who are already friendly and engaged: they give feedback without being chased, they actually want the product to get better, and they use it enough that there's something real to watch. A team that's at least partly in one office is ideal, because the point is to see people work, together, the way they normally do.

## Plan it well

A good visit is prepared for, not improvised.

1. **Know what you're going in to learn.** Go through the [support signal](/handbook/support-and-care), past calls, and what you've heard from [listening to users](/handbook/listening-to-users), and write down the pressing issues and the things you're most curious about.
2. **Find one point of contact** on their side to coordinate. Two or three days is usually the right length: enough for real time with people, not so much that you're underfoot. Tying it to a moment they're together anyway, like their own offsite, works well.
3. **Sort the logistics early.** Book travel ahead, and clear the budget with People and Ops the way [spending money](/handbook/spending-money) describes. This is normal, encouraged spending, not a favor you have to justify.
4. **Set a light agenda.** Block an hour each with a few different users. Offer something useful in return, a short training session or an open Q&A, so it's worth their time too.
5. **Do your homework.** Watch how they actually use the product before you go, so you're asking sharp questions instead of the ones five minutes of looking would have answered.

## While you're there

Let people show you, don't present at them. Ask someone to do a normal task and watch where they hesitate, where they work around something, where they expected a thing to be and it wasn't. That hesitation is the gold.

<Callout type="brand">
  If you can fix a small thing and ship it while you're still sitting there, do it. Turning "this annoys me" into "it's fixed, refresh the page" in the same afternoon is the single most convincing thing you can do in the room.
</Callout>

Be generous with your help, even on things outside the part of the product you own. You're the face of the whole company for those few days, and [owning what you build](/handbook/feature-ownership) stretches a little wider than usual while you're a guest.

## After you're home

The visit isn't done when you fly back. Write up what you learned and share it with your team, and be willing to re-order what you were planning to build in light of it, since you now know something the roadmap didn't. Then actually do the things: ship the fixes, and tell them you did, listing what changed because of their time. Following up in the weeks after is what turns a nice visit into a customer who trusts you, and it's the same [product engineering](/handbook/product-engineering) instinct as everything else: talk to users, then close the loop.

docs.title: Where we're going
docs.description: Our direction and what winning looks like, without a dated roadmap.
headings: People who are proud to work here
Direction, not a promise about products
docs.body:
People expect this page to be a roadmap: a list of features with quarters next to them. It isn't, and it won't be. We keep a [public roadmap](/roadmap) for what we're building; this page is about the direction underneath it. Dated roadmaps age badly and mostly exist to make a company look decisive on a slide. What we can tell you honestly is the kind of company we're building toward, and how we'd know we were succeeding. That's more durable than a Gantt chart, and it's the part that actually steers the decisions.

## The company we're building toward

We're building a small software company that's still here in ten years, still making things people are glad to use, still run in the open. Not the biggest, not the loudest, not the one with the flashiest funding announcement. The one that's good, and stays good, and that people trust because it's earned it over a long time.

That's a specific ambition, not a modest one. Plenty of companies get big. Very few stay good while doing it. We'd rather be the second kind. This is what [the long game](/handbook/values#the-long-game) means in practice: we optimize for still being proud of this years from now, which rules out a lot of tempting shortcuts today.

## How we'd know we're winning

Growth charts are easy to game and easy to fake, so we don't treat them as the scoreboard. Here's what we actually watch.

**Craft that holds up.** The real test isn't whether the demo dazzles. It's whether the thing still feels good to use a year in, when the novelty's gone and it's just part of your day. Work that ages well is the hardest kind to fake, so it's the kind we measure ourselves against.

**Trust you can measure by reading us.** Because we work in the open, anyone can check whether we do what we say. If the handbook and the behavior match, if you can read our reasoning and find it honest, that's a form of winning that doesn't show up in revenue. We want to be a company you can audit and come away trusting more, not less.

**Durability.** Can we survive a bad quarter without abandoning our principles? Can we say no to money that would cost us the values? A company that only holds its line when times are good doesn't really have a line. Winning is being the kind of business that stays itself under pressure.

<Callout type="brand" title="The scoreboard we care about">
  Would the people who use our work be genuinely sad if we disappeared? Would
  the people who build it be proud to say they did? If both are yes, we're
  winning, whatever the chart says.
</Callout>

## People who are proud to work here

The other half of "where we're going" is who's coming with us. We want Flagon to be a place a small crew of capable people are genuinely proud to be part of, because the work is good, the treatment is fair, and nobody has to leave their integrity at the door.

That's a real constraint on how we grow. We'd rather stay small and be somewhere people are proud of than get big and become somewhere people tolerate. If growing means turning this into a place we wouldn't recommend to a friend, then growing that way is off the table.

## Direction, not a promise about products

Notice what this page doesn't do: it doesn't name a specific product, a date, or a feature. That's deliberate. What we make will change as we learn, and pinning ourselves to a wall of dated promises is exactly the kind of showmanship we try to avoid. See [built in public](/handbook/values) for why.

What won't change is the direction: good things, made honestly, for the long term, by people who are proud to make them. Everything specific serves that. If you want to hold us to something, hold us to this.

docs.title: Which products to build
docs.description: How we decide what to build, starting from the foundation and building up, never sideways into a worse version of five other tools.
headings: Sync is the point, not a plugin
docs.body:
Deciding what to build is mostly deciding what not to. Here's the rule we hold ourselves to, so the decision isn't remade from scratch every time a good-sounding idea shows up. The day-to-day version of this, the way a team sets its priorities, is [deciding what to build](/handbook/deciding-what-to-build).

## Start at the foundation

Flagon begins as a multi-tenant platform where people define and manage their products and teams. That is the foundation, and it comes first, done properly, before anything clever gets built on top of it. Tenancy, ownership, and the core model of products and teams are the thing everything else depends on, so they get the care of a foundation, not the speed of a feature.

## Build up, not sideways

Once the foundation holds, we add the things that make it more useful: keeping definitions in sync, an API and SDKs to build against, access control, history. What we don't do is wander sideways into unrelated features because a competitor has them. A pile of features bolted onto the side just makes us a worse version of five other tools. If it doesn't make products and teams as a source of truth more true, more useful, or more trustworthy, it's a no, even when it's a good idea in the abstract.

## Sync is the point, not a plugin

The definitions have to stay true in the tools people already live in. So synchronization, in both directions, is foundational work. We don't treat it as an integration to bolt on once the "real" product is done. Being the source of truth means nothing if the truth can't reach the places that need it.

## We decide in the open

None of this happens behind a curtain. What we're weighing, what we've committed to, and what we've said no to lives on the public [roadmap](/roadmap), and the reasoning gets written down the same way we [make every other decision](/handbook/decisions). If we change our minds, you'll see why.

docs.title: Who we build for
docs.description: The teams Flagon is for, the person who feels the problem first, and who we're honestly not for.
headings: The person who feels it first
docs.body:
We build for the people responsible for how a software organization is put together: its products, its teams, who owns what, and how all of that stays true across the dozen other tools that each think they own the answer.

## The team we build for

Growing software companies where the shape of the org matters and keeps drifting. Products get renamed, teams reorganize, ownership changes, and the truth of it ends up smeared across a spreadsheet, a wiki, an identity provider, and three tools that each hold a slightly different version. Somebody spends their week reconciling that by hand, and it's still wrong by Friday.

That somebody, and the platform, engineering, and operations leaders who feel the cost of it, are who we build for.

## The person who feels it first

Usually an engineer or a platform person. They want products and teams defined once, in a system built to be the source of truth, and they want every other tool to sync with that instead of drifting from it. They don't want another place to re-enter the same org chart. They want the place the org chart actually lives, that the rest of their stack agrees with.

We go hard on making that person's life better first. Get it right for them, and the value spreads to everyone downstream who was quietly paying for the drift.

## Who we're not for

A tiny team where a shared doc is genuinely enough. If the shape of your org fits in your head, you don't need us yet, and we'd rather say so than sell you something you'll resent.

Organizations that want a locked box with no way out, either. Your definitions are yours, sync goes both directions, and export is always on the table. If lock-in is the point for you, we're the wrong choice. The fuller version of that honesty is on [who Flagon is for, and who it isn't](/not-for-everyone).

docs.title: Why Flagon exists
docs.description: The reason we started, and the one bet the whole company runs on.
docs.body:
There is already plenty of software, and plenty of companies making it. We started another one anyway. Here is why.

## Why we started

We wanted to work somewhere that operated the way we thought a company should, and it was easier to build one than to keep waiting for it to appear.

Most of us have worked at places where the stated values and the actual behavior drifted apart: the handbook said one thing, the calendar said another, and decisions arrived as law from rooms you were never in. None of that is unusual. It is just tiring, and it makes the software worse, because the people closest to the work stop bothering to have opinions. Flagon is the attempt to not do that. Not a manifesto about it, an actual company, run out loud so you can check whether we mean it.

## The one bet

Everything here rests on a single bet: that building in the open is an advantage, not a liability.

Trust is not something you buy with a marketing budget. It is a track record someone can read. So we publish the track record as we go, the [handbook](/handbook), the [roadmap](/roadmap), the reasoning, the misfires, and when we get something wrong the wrong version stays in the git history. Working this way makes the work sharper too: a decision you have to defend in public tends to lose its weak points before it ships. That is the whole thesis. The rest of this handbook is what it looks like in practice.

## What we are not doing

We are not optimizing for a quick exit. There is no acquisition we are steering toward and no plan to flip this to someone bigger. The goal is boring and hard: to still be here in a decade, still making good things, still a company worth working at. That one choice quietly settles a lot of the others, from [how we pay people](/handbook/compensation) to [how we make money](/handbook/how-we-make-money) to how fast we grow. It's [one of our values](/handbook/values#the-long-game), and the reason [staying alive](/handbook/staying-alive) matters more than looking impressive.

If watching a company try to do this in public sounds interesting rather than terrifying, you are probably our kind of person.

docs.title: Working async
docs.description: Non-linear workdays, written-first by default, and why async is what makes remote humane.
headings: Your day is yours to arrange
Write so nobody has to be online at once
What a reasonable reply looks like
Why this is the humane version
docs.body:
[How we communicate](/handbook/communication) covers the tone and the tools. This page is about the shape of the day. Async isn't a communication style we picked for flavor.
